name: Life Sciences
tagline: The living world, from the cell to the biosphere.

nodes.title: Living and Not Living
nodes.goal: Tell what is alive and what is not.
nodes.kid_text: Living things eat, grow, and move all by themselves. A puppy drinks milk, gets bigger, and runs to you, so it is alive! But your toy truck can only move when you push it, so it is not living. Look around you and find which things eat and grow.

quiz.prompt: Which one is alive? 🐛 🪨 🧸
quiz.say: Which one is alive? The caterpillar, the rock, or the teddy bear?
quiz.explain: The caterpillar eats and grows, so it is alive. The rock and the teddy bear never do.

quiz.prompt: Which one is alive? 🌳 🚗 🎈
quiz.say: Which one is alive? The tree, the car, or the balloon?
quiz.explain: A tree is alive! It drinks water and grows, even though it cannot walk.

quiz.prompt: Which grows bigger by itself? 🌱 🧸 🥄
quiz.say: Which one grows bigger all by itself? The little sprout, the teddy bear, or the spoon?
quiz.explain: Only the sprout grows. Toys and spoons stay exactly the same size.

quiz.prompt: Is a tree alive? 🌳
choices: Yes
No
quiz.answer: Yes
quiz.say: Is a tree alive? Say yes, or no.
quiz.explain: Yes! A tree drinks water, grows tall, and makes seeds, so it is living.

quiz.prompt: Which one needs food and water?
choices: Puppy
Toy robot
River
quiz.answer: Puppy
quiz.say: Which one needs food and water to stay alive? A puppy, a toy robot, or a river?
quiz.explain: The puppy eats and drinks. A toy robot moves, but it never gets hungry.

quiz.prompt: Which one can have babies?
choices: Hen
Car
Cloud
quiz.answer: Hen
quiz.say: Which one can have babies? A hen, a car, or a cloud?
quiz.explain: Living things make babies. A hen lays eggs that hatch into chicks.

quiz.prompt: Which one drinks water?
choices: Horse
Balloon
Snowman
quiz.answer: Horse
quiz.say: Which one drinks water? A horse, a balloon, or a snowman?
quiz.explain: The horse is living, so it drinks. A snowman is made of water but never drinks.

lesson_media.alt: A plant and animal satisfy several linked signs of life, while a rock lacks cells, metabolism, response, and reproduction.
lesson_media.caption: Living things are identified by a coordinated set of processes—not simply by motion, size, or any single visible clue.

nodes.title: Animals
nodes.goal: Name common animals and where they live.
nodes.kid_text: Animals live in all sorts of homes. A fish swishes its tail in the water, a bird builds a cozy nest up in a tree, and a cow munches grass in a green field. When you meet an animal, ask where it likes to live, the water, the sky, or the ground.

quiz.prompt: Where does a fish live? 🐟
choices: Water
Nest
Cave
quiz.answer: Water
quiz.say: Where does a fish live? In the water, in a nest, or in a cave?
quiz.explain: A fish swishes its tail in the water and breathes there too.

quiz.prompt: Who lives in a hive? 🍯
quiz.say: Who lives in a busy hive? The bee, the ant, or the butterfly?
quiz.explain: Bees live together in a hive. Ants live in a nest under the ground.

quiz.prompt: Who lays eggs in a nest in a tree?
choices: Bird
Frog
Cat
quiz.answer: Bird
quiz.say: Who lays eggs in a nest up in a tree? A bird, a frog, or a cat?
quiz.explain: Birds build nests in trees. Frogs lay eggs too, but in the water.

quiz.prompt: Where does a frog live? 🐸
choices: Pond
Ocean
Desert
quiz.answer: Pond
quiz.say: Where does a frog like to live? In a pond, in the ocean, or in the desert?
quiz.explain: Frogs live in fresh water ponds. The ocean is far too salty for them.

quiz.prompt: Which animal has no legs? 🐍 🦎 🐛
quiz.say: Which animal has no legs at all? The snake, the lizard, or the caterpillar?
quiz.explain: A snake has no legs and slides along. Lizards and caterpillars both have legs.

quiz.prompt: Which animal can fly?
choices: Bat
Penguin
Rabbit
quiz.answer: Bat
quiz.say: Which animal can fly? A bat, a penguin, or a rabbit?
quiz.explain: A bat has wings and flies at night. A penguin has wings but only swims with them.

quiz.prompt: Which animal says moo? 🐄
choices: Cow
Goat
Sheep
quiz.answer: Cow
quiz.say: Which animal says moo? A cow, a goat, or a sheep?
quiz.explain: The cow says moo. The sheep says baa and the goat says maa.

lesson_media.alt: Fish, bird, and camel examples connect gills, wings, and water-saving traits to the different resources and challenges of their habitats.
lesson_media.caption: Animals do not merely live in named places—their structures and behaviours solve particular problems posed by those environments.

nodes.title: Plants Grow
nodes.goal: Watch seeds become plants.
nodes.kid_text: A tiny seed can grow into a big plant! If you tuck a bean seed into the dirt and give it water and sunshine, a little green sprout will pop up. Wait a few more days and it grows taller and taller. Every giant tree started as a small seed just like that.

quiz.prompt: Which one can grow into a plant?
choices: Seed
Pebble
Bead
quiz.answer: Seed
quiz.say: Which one can grow into a plant? A seed, a pebble, or a bead?
quiz.explain: Only the seed is living inside, so only the seed can grow.

quiz.prompt: What does a seed need to grow? 🌱
choices: Water
Milk
Sand
quiz.answer: Water
quiz.say: What does a seed need to grow? Water, milk, or sand?
quiz.explain: Seeds drink water from the soil. Milk is for baby animals, not for plants.

quiz.prompt: Which comes first? 🌰 🌱 🌳
quiz.say: Which one comes first? The seed, the sprout, or the big tree?
quiz.explain: Every big tree started out as a tiny seed.

quiz.prompt: Which comes last? 🌰 🌱 🌳
quiz.say: Which one comes last, after lots of growing? The seed, the sprout, or the big tree?
quiz.explain: First a seed, then a sprout, and last of all a big tree.

quiz.prompt: What else does a sprout need? 🪴
choices: Sunlight
The dark
Ice
quiz.answer: Sunlight
quiz.say: What else does a little sprout need to grow tall? Sunlight, the dark, or ice?
quiz.explain: A sprout needs sunlight. Seeds start in the dark soil, but sprouts need light.

quiz.prompt: Where do you plant a seed?
choices: Soil
Dry sand
A box
quiz.answer: Soil
quiz.say: Where do you plant a seed so it can grow? In soil, in dry sand, or in a box?
quiz.explain: Soil holds the water and food a seed needs. Dry sand has no water in it.

quiz.prompt: Are plants living things? 🌳
choices: Yes
No
quiz.answer: Yes
quiz.say: Are plants living things? Say yes, or no.
quiz.explain: Yes! Plants grow, drink water, and make new plants, so they are alive.

lesson_media.alt: A four-stage plant life cycle shows a seed germinating root-first, producing leaves, flowering, and making seeds that restart the cycle.
lesson_media.caption: The diagram separates germination from later photosynthetic growth and shows why seed formation closes, rather than ends, the life cycle.

nodes.title: My Body
nodes.goal: Name body parts and the five senses.
nodes.kid_text: Your body has special parts that help you every single day. You see with your eyes, hear with your ears, smell with your nose, taste with your tongue, and touch with your fingers. Those are your five senses! Try closing your eyes and use your ears to hear what is near you.

quiz.prompt: What do you see with? 🌈
choices: Eyes
Ears
Nose
quiz.answer: Eyes
quiz.say: What do you see with? Your eyes, your ears, or your nose?
quiz.explain: Your eyes help you see everything around you.

quiz.prompt: A bell rings. You hear it with your... 🔔
choices: Ears
Nose
Hands
quiz.answer: Ears
quiz.say: A bell rings. You hear it with your what? Your ears, your nose, or your hands?
quiz.explain: Your ears catch every sound, even very quiet ones.

quiz.prompt: What tastes ice cream? 🍦
choices: Tongue
Teeth
Nose
quiz.answer: Tongue
quiz.say: What part of you tastes the ice cream? Your tongue, your teeth, or your nose?
quiz.explain: Your tongue tastes sweet things. Your teeth only chew.

quiz.prompt: What do you smell with? 🌷
choices: Nose
Tongue
Ears
quiz.answer: Nose
quiz.say: What do you smell flowers with? Your nose, your tongue, or your ears?
quiz.explain: Your nose sniffs smells, like warm cookies baking.

quiz.prompt: What feels soft fur? 🐈
choices: Fingers
Eyes
Hair
quiz.answer: Fingers
quiz.say: What part of you feels soft fur? Your fingers, your eyes, or your hair?
quiz.explain: Your fingers touch things and tell you if they are soft or bumpy.

quiz.prompt: How many senses do you have? 🧒
quiz.say: How many senses does your body have? Is it 3, or 5, or 7?
quiz.explain: You have five senses: see, hear, smell, taste, and touch.

quiz.prompt: Which part bends when you walk?
choices: Knee
Elbow
Wrist
quiz.answer: Knee
quiz.say: Which part of you bends when you walk? Your knee, your elbow, or your wrist?
quiz.explain: Your knee bends in the middle of your leg. Your elbow bends in your arm.

lesson_media.alt: A five-row table maps sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch to their organs, detected stimuli, and nervous-system destination.
lesson_media.caption: The five senses are different input channels: each is specialised for a stimulus, yet all communicate through the nervous system.

nodes.title: The Seasons
nodes.goal: Notice how living things change with the seasons.
nodes.kid_text: The year has four seasons, and living things change with each one. In spring, flowers bloom and baby animals are born, and summer is warm and green. In fall, leaves turn orange and drift down, and in cold winter some animals curl up to sleep. Peek outside, which season do you see today?

quiz.prompt: When do leaves turn orange? 🍂
choices: Fall
Spring
Summer
quiz.answer: Fall
quiz.say: When do the leaves turn orange and drift down? In fall, in spring, or in summer?
quiz.explain: In fall the leaves turn orange and drop off the trees.

quiz.prompt: Which season is snowy? ❄️
choices: Winter
Fall
Spring
quiz.answer: Winter
quiz.say: Which season is cold and snowy? Winter, fall, or spring?
quiz.explain: Winter is the coldest season, when snow can fall.

quiz.prompt: When are baby animals born? 🐣🌷
choices: Spring
Fall
Winter
quiz.answer: Spring
quiz.say: When are lots of baby animals born? In spring, in fall, or in winter?
quiz.explain: In spring it warms up, flowers bloom, and baby animals are born.

quiz.prompt: Which season is hottest? ☀️
choices: Summer
Spring
Fall
quiz.answer: Summer
quiz.say: Which season is the hottest of them all? Summer, spring, or fall?
quiz.explain: Summer is the hottest. Spring is warm, but summer is warmer still.

quiz.prompt: How many seasons in a year? 📅
quiz.say: How many seasons are there in one year? Is it 4, or 2, or 7?
quiz.explain: There are four seasons: spring, summer, fall, and winter.

quiz.prompt: Bears sleep through which season? 🐻
choices: Winter
Summer
Spring
quiz.answer: Winter
quiz.say: Which season do bears sleep through? Winter, summer, or spring?
quiz.explain: Bears sleep through the cold winter, when food is hard to find.

quiz.prompt: When do many birds fly south? 🐦
choices: Fall
Spring
Summer
quiz.answer: Fall
quiz.say: When do many birds fly away to warmer places? In fall, in spring, or in summer?
quiz.explain: Birds fly south in fall, before the cold comes, and they come back in spring.

lesson_media.alt: A spring-to-winter cycle links changing daylight and temperature to budding, growth, leaf fall, migration, and dormancy in living things.
lesson_media.caption: Living things use seasonal cues to time costly activities so growth and reproduction occur when resources are more favourable.

nodes.title: Life Cycles
nodes.goal: Egg to frog, caterpillar to butterfly.
nodes.kid_text: A life cycle is the repeating sequence from a new individual through growth, adulthood and reproduction. Frog eggs hatch into legless tadpoles; tadpoles develop legs, become froglets and mature into adult frogs that can produce eggs. A caterpillar changes into a pupa called a chrysalis before an adult butterfly emerges and can lay eggs. These large changes in body form are called metamorphosis. Dogs grow and develop too, but without metamorphosis.

lesson_media.alt: An adult frog produces eggs; eggs hatch into a tadpole; the tadpole becomes a four-legged froglet; the froglet matures into an adult.
lesson_media.caption: The repeating stages form a life cycle; the tadpole-to-frog transformation is metamorphosis.

lesson_media.title: Follow a life cycle
lesson_media.instructions: Choose an animal and move forward through its stages. Notice which animals undergo metamorphosis and how every cycle reaches a new generation.

quiz.prompt: A tadpole grows up into a...
quiz.say: A wiggly tadpole grows up into what? A frog, a fish, or a lizard?
quiz.explain: A tadpole swims like a fish, but it grows legs and becomes a frog.

quiz.prompt: A caterpillar becomes a... 🐛
quiz.say: A caterpillar becomes a pupa called a chrysalis. What adult emerges later? A butterfly, a bee, or a ladybug?
quiz.explain: The caterpillar changes into a pupa called a chrysalis, and an adult butterfly later emerges.

quiz.prompt: Which stage does a new frog individual begin as?
choices: Egg
Tadpole
Frog
quiz.answer: Egg
quiz.say: Which stage does a new frog individual begin as? An egg, a tadpole, or an adult frog?
quiz.explain: A frog starts as a tiny egg, and the egg hatches into a tadpole.

quiz.prompt: What can hatch from a fertilized, developing hen's egg? 🥚
quiz.say: What can hatch from a fertilized, developing hen's egg? A chick, a snake, or a caterpillar?
quiz.explain: A fertilized hen's egg can develop and hatch into a chick. Snakes hatch from their own species' eggs.

quiz.prompt: Which stage does a new butterfly individual begin as?
quiz.say: Which stage does a new butterfly individual begin as? The egg, the caterpillar, or the adult butterfly?
quiz.explain: A new individual begins as an egg, then develops through caterpillar and chrysalis stages into an adult that can lay eggs.

quiz.prompt: What does a tadpole grow? 🐸
choices: Legs
Wings
Feathers
quiz.answer: Legs
quiz.say: What does a tadpole grow as it turns into a frog? Legs, wings, or feathers?
quiz.explain: During metamorphosis, a tadpole develops hind legs and then front legs as its body becomes frog-like.

quiz.prompt: A puppy grows into a... 🐶
choices: Dog
Wolf
Kitten
quiz.answer: Dog
quiz.say: A puppy grows up into what? A dog, a wolf, or a kitten?
quiz.explain: A puppy grows and its proportions change gradually into an adult dog, without undergoing metamorphosis.

nodes.title: Habitats
nodes.goal: How animals fit their homes.
nodes.kid_text: A habitat is the home where an animal finds food, water, and a safe place to rest. A polar bear has thick warm fur that fits its icy home, and a camel can go a long time without water in the hot, sandy desert. Each animal's body is just right for where it lives. What would help you live in a snowy place?

quiz.prompt: Who has thick fur for icy places? ❄️
choices: Polar bear
Brown bear
Camel
quiz.answer: Polar bear
quiz.say: Who has thick white fur for a cold, icy home? A polar bear, a brown bear, or a camel?
quiz.explain: The polar bear's thick fur and fat keep it warm out on the ice.

quiz.prompt: Where does a camel live? 🐫
choices: Desert
Rainforest
Ocean
quiz.answer: Desert
quiz.say: Where does a camel live? In the desert, in the rainforest, or in the ocean?
quiz.explain: Camels live in the hot, dry desert, where there is very little water.

quiz.prompt: A fish needs a home with...
choices: Water
Sand
Grass
quiz.answer: Water
quiz.say: A fish needs a home with what? Water, sand, or grass?
quiz.explain: A fish breathes and swims in water, so water is its home.

quiz.prompt: Where does a monkey live? 🐒
choices: Trees
Caves
Under the ground
quiz.answer: Trees
quiz.say: Where does a monkey live? In the trees, in caves, or under the ground?
quiz.explain: Monkeys live in trees, where they swing between branches and find fruit.

quiz.prompt: Who lives in the salty ocean? 🌊
quiz.say: Who lives out in the salty ocean? The dolphin, the crocodile, or the camel?
quiz.explain: Dolphins live in the ocean. Crocodiles live in rivers and swamps instead.

quiz.prompt: A duck's webbed feet help it... 🦆
choices: Swim
Dig
Climb
quiz.answer: Swim
quiz.say: A duck has wide webbed feet. Do they help it swim, dig, or climb?
quiz.explain: Flat webbed feet push against the water, so ducks swim well.

quiz.prompt: Whose home is a cave? 🦇
choices: Bat
Squirrel
Fish
quiz.answer: Bat
quiz.say: Whose home is a dark cave? A bat, a squirrel, or a fish?
quiz.explain: Bats sleep in caves by day. Squirrels sleep up in trees instead.

lesson_media.alt: Desert, ocean, and polar cards pair environmental challenges with cactus, fish, and mammal adaptations that address those challenges.
lesson_media.caption: Habitats act as filters: inherited traits that improve survival and reproduction under local conditions tend to persist.

nodes.title: Food Chains
nodes.goal: Who eats whom, and where energy goes.
nodes.kid_text: A food chain shows who eats whom. The sun helps grass grow, a rabbit eats the grass, and a fox eats the rabbit, so energy passes along like links in a chain. Plants always start the chain because they make their own food from sunlight. Can you build a food chain with a leaf, a caterpillar, and a bird?

quiz.prompt: What does a rabbit eat? 🐰
choices: Grass
Mice
Fish
quiz.answer: Grass
quiz.say: What does a rabbit eat? Grass, mice, or fish?
quiz.explain: Rabbits eat only plants, like grass and leaves.

quiz.prompt: What starts every food chain?
choices: Sun
Soil
Fox
quiz.answer: Sun
quiz.say: What starts every food chain? The sun, the soil, or the fox?
quiz.explain: The sun comes first. Plants use sunlight to make food, and animals eat the plants.

quiz.prompt: A caterpillar eats a leaf. Who eats it?
choices: Bird
Rabbit
Cow
quiz.answer: Bird
quiz.say: The caterpillar eats the leaf. Who eats the caterpillar? A bird, a rabbit, or a cow?
quiz.explain: A bird eats the caterpillar. Rabbits and cows eat plants, not caterpillars.

quiz.prompt: Who eats a little fish? 🐟
choices: Shark
Seaweed
Snail
quiz.answer: Shark
quiz.say: Who eats the little fish? A shark, some seaweed, or a snail?
quiz.explain: The shark eats the fish, and the food chain keeps going.

quiz.prompt: Plants make their own food from...
choices: Sunlight
Soil
Meat
quiz.answer: Sunlight
quiz.say: What do plants use to make their own food? Sunlight, soil, or meat?
quiz.explain: Plants make food from sunlight. Soil gives them water, but not food.

quiz.prompt: Grass, then a mouse, then a big bird. Who eats last?
choices: Owl
Mouse
Grass
quiz.answer: Owl
quiz.say: Grass, then a mouse, then a big bird. Who eats last? The owl, the mouse, or the grass?
quiz.explain: The owl eats last, because it eats the mouse that ate the grass.

quiz.prompt: Which animal eats only plants?
choices: Rabbit
Fox
Owl
quiz.answer: Rabbit
quiz.say: Which animal eats only plants? A rabbit, a fox, or an owl?
quiz.explain: Rabbits eat only plants. Foxes and owls both hunt other animals.

lesson_media.alt: A labelled network sends energy from sunlight to grass, rabbit, and fox, while dead matter and waste flow to decomposers.
lesson_media.caption: Food-chain arrows track transferred energy, whereas decomposers reveal the different fate of matter: nutrients are recycled but energy is not.

nodes.title: Parts of a Plant
nodes.goal: Roots, stems, leaves, flowers and their jobs.
nodes.kid_text: Every part of a plant has an important job. The roots dig down to drink water from the soil, the stem holds the plant up straight, the leaves catch sunlight to make food, and the flowers make seeds for new plants. Next time you spot a plant, try naming each part and the job it does.

quiz.prompt: Which part drinks water from soil?
choices: Roots
Stem
Leaf
quiz.answer: Roots
quiz.say: Which part of a plant drinks water from the soil? The roots, the stem, or the leaf?
quiz.explain: The roots drink the water, and the stem carries it up to the rest of the plant.

quiz.prompt: Which part catches sunlight? ☀️
choices: Leaves
Roots
Flower
quiz.answer: Leaves
quiz.say: Which part catches the sunlight to make food? The leaves, the roots, or the flower?
quiz.explain: Flat green leaves catch sunlight and turn it into food.

quiz.prompt: Which part makes seeds? 🌱
choices: Flower
Leaf
Stem
quiz.answer: Flower
quiz.say: Which part of a plant makes seeds? The flower, the leaf, or the stem?
quiz.explain: Flowers make the seeds that grow into new plants.

quiz.prompt: Which part holds the plant up?
choices: Stem
Root
Petal
quiz.answer: Stem
quiz.say: Which part holds the plant up straight? The stem, the root, or the petal?
quiz.explain: The stem is like a strong pole holding the plant up.

quiz.prompt: A carrot is which part? 🥕
choices: Root
Stem
Fruit
quiz.answer: Root
quiz.say: A carrot is which part of the plant? The root, the stem, or the fruit?
quiz.explain: A carrot is a fat root that grew under the ground.

quiz.prompt: Which part carries water up?
choices: Stem
Roots
Petals
quiz.answer: Stem
quiz.say: Which part carries water up to the leaves? The stem, the roots, or the petals?
quiz.explain: The roots drink the water, and the stem carries it up like a straw.

quiz.prompt: An apple grows from which part? 🍎
choices: Flower
Leaf
Root
quiz.answer: Flower
quiz.say: An apple grows from which part of the tree? The flower, the leaf, or the root?
quiz.explain: Each apple grows where a flower used to be, and it holds the seeds inside.

lesson_media.alt: A plant transport network traces water from soil through roots and xylem to leaves, then sugar through phloem to flowers and growing tissues.
lesson_media.caption: Plant parts cooperate: roots acquire materials, leaves build sugars, vascular tissues transport them, and flowers support reproduction.

nodes.title: Inside the Body
nodes.goal: Bones, muscles, heart and lungs.
nodes.kid_text: Inside you are busy parts you cannot see. Your hard bones hold you up like a frame, and your muscles pull on them so you can run and jump. Your heart squeezes to push blood all around you, and your lungs fill up like balloons every time you breathe. Put your hand on your chest, can you feel your heart beating?

quiz.prompt: What pushes blood around you? 🏃
choices: Heart
Lungs
Stomach
quiz.answer: Heart
quiz.say: What pushes blood all around your body? Your heart, your lungs, or your stomach?
quiz.explain: Your heart squeezes over and over and pushes blood everywhere.

quiz.prompt: What fills with air when you breathe?
choices: Lungs
Heart
Stomach
quiz.answer: Lungs
quiz.say: What fills up with air when you breathe in? Your lungs, your heart, or your stomach?
quiz.explain: Your lungs fill up like two balloons with every breath.

quiz.prompt: What holds your body up? 🧍
choices: Bones
Muscles
Skin
quiz.answer: Bones
quiz.say: What holds your body up like a frame? Your bones, your muscles, or your skin?
quiz.explain: Hard bones hold you up, and muscles pull on the bones to move them.

quiz.prompt: What lets you lift and jump? 🏀
choices: Muscles
Bones
Lungs
quiz.answer: Muscles
quiz.say: What lets you lift things and jump high? Your muscles, your bones, or your lungs?
quiz.explain: Muscles squeeze and pull your bones so you can move.

quiz.prompt: Where do you feel your heartbeat?
choices: Chest
Tummy
Knee
quiz.answer: Chest
quiz.say: Where can you feel your heart beating? In your chest, your tummy, or your knee?
quiz.explain: Put your hand on your chest and you can feel the thump, thump.

quiz.prompt: Where does food go when you swallow?
choices: Stomach
Lungs
Heart
quiz.answer: Stomach
quiz.say: Where does your food go after you swallow it? Your stomach, your lungs, or your heart?
quiz.explain: Food slides down to your stomach. Only air goes down to your lungs.

quiz.prompt: What sends messages to your body? 📣
choices: Brain
Heart
Bones
quiz.answer: Brain
quiz.say: What sends messages telling your body what to do? Your brain, your heart, or your bones?
quiz.explain: Your brain sends messages so your body knows how to move.

lesson_media.alt: A body-system route carries oxygen from air through lungs and heart to muscle, returns carbon dioxide, and links muscles with bones for movement.
lesson_media.caption: Organs form coordinated systems; none of the lungs, heart, muscles, or skeleton can supply movement by working alone.

nodes.title: Staying Healthy
nodes.goal: Food, sleep, exercise and hygiene.
nodes.kid_text: You can help your body stay strong and healthy. Eat colorful fruits and vegetables, drink water, and run and play to build strong muscles. Get plenty of sleep at night so your body can rest and grow, and wash your hands to keep germs away. Little healthy choices every day keep you feeling great!

quiz.prompt: Which helps you grow strong? 🥦 🍬 🍟
quiz.say: Which one helps your body grow strong? The broccoli, the candy, or the fries?
quiz.explain: Vegetables like broccoli give your body what it needs to grow.

quiz.prompt: When does your body rest and grow? 🌙
choices: Sleep
Running
Watching TV
quiz.answer: Sleep
quiz.say: When does your body rest and grow? During sleep, while running, or while watching TV?
quiz.explain: Sleeping at night is when your body rests and grows.

quiz.prompt: What gets germs off your hands? 🦠
choices: Soap and water
Just water
Wiping your shirt
quiz.answer: Soap and water
quiz.say: What really gets germs off your hands? Soap and water, just water, or wiping your shirt?
quiz.explain: Soap and water washes germs away. Water on its own leaves lots of germs behind.

quiz.prompt: Best drink for your body? 🏃
choices: Water
Soda
Juice
quiz.answer: Water
quiz.say: Which drink is best for your body? Water, soda, or juice?
quiz.explain: Water is best. Soda and juice both have lots of sugar in them.

quiz.prompt: Which builds strong muscles?
choices: Running
Sitting
Sleeping
quiz.answer: Running
quiz.say: Which one builds strong muscles? Running, sitting, or sleeping?
quiz.explain: Moving and running makes your muscles stronger.

quiz.prompt: Where should you sneeze? 🤧
choices: Into your elbow
Into your hands
Into the air
quiz.answer: Into your elbow
quiz.say: Where should you sneeze? Into your elbow, into your hands, or into the air?
quiz.explain: Sneeze into your elbow. Your hands touch everything, so germs spread from them.

quiz.prompt: Hours of sleep kids need? 😴
quiz.say: How many hours of sleep do kids need each night? Is it 10, or 4, or 16?
quiz.explain: Kids need about ten hours of sleep each night to grow and feel good.

lesson_media.alt: A table links varied food, sleep, activity, and hygiene to the resources or challenges they provide and the body functions they support.
lesson_media.caption: The habits work through different mechanisms, so a single 'healthy' action cannot substitute for nutrition, sleep, movement, and hygiene together.

nodes.title: Cells
nodes.goal: Living organisms are built from one or more cells, the basic units of life.

lesson_media.alt: Three schematic microscope fields show rectangular onion-bulb epidermal cells with walls and nuclei, green leaf cells with walls and chloroplasts, and irregular pink cheek cells with nuclei and no walls.
lesson_media.caption: Cell structures vary by specimen; these schematic fields use different views and are not to scale.

lesson_media.title: Compare cells under a microscope
lesson_media.instructions: Switch between onion-bulb, green-leaf and cheek specimens, then change magnification. Notice which visible structures belong to each specimen and which details are schematic.

quiz.prompt: Which statement best describes the role of cells in living things?
quiz.answer: Cells are the basic building units that all living things are made of
quiz.explain: All living organisms are built from one or more cells, the smallest unit of life.
choices: Cells are the basic building units that all living things are made of
Cells are non-living minerals absorbed from the food we eat
Cells are found in animals but not in plants or fungi
A living thing is made of one cell, however big it is

quiz.prompt: Why can't you see a single human skin cell using just your eyes?
quiz.answer: Cells are far too small for the eye without a microscope
quiz.explain: A human skin cell is a few hundredths of a millimetre across, well below what the unaided eye can resolve. A microscope magnifies it enough to be seen, and a stain then makes its edges stand out.
choices: Skin cells are transparent like glass, reflecting no light
Cells are far too small for the eye without a microscope
Skin is made of flat sheets of protein, not of cells
Skin cells are joined so tightly that no gaps show

quiz.prompt: Blood cells, muscle cells and the cells in onion epidermis all look different. Name one structure that surrounds every one of them.
quiz.answer: Each is surrounded by a cell membrane.
quiz.explain: Every cell has a cell membrane around its contents. Onion epidermal cells also have a rigid cell wall outside that membrane.

quiz.prompt: Under a microscope, onion-bulb epidermal cells form neat rows with firm box-like outlines, while cheek cells have thinner, irregular outlines. What best explains the firm onion-cell shape?
quiz.answer: Plant cells have a stiff wall outside their membrane
choices: Cheek cells were squashed flat when they were scraped
Cheek cells are much younger than the onion cells are
Plant cells have a stiff wall outside their membrane
Onion cells are dead, so they have dried into boxes
quiz.explain: A plant cell has a rigid cellulose wall outside its membrane, supporting its outline and helping neighbours pack into rows. Cheek cells lack a wall; their flexible outlines depend on the membrane, cytoskeleton and surrounding tissue rather than a default rounded shape.

quiz.prompt: In a typical plant or animal cell, where is most of the DNA that guides growth and work stored?
quiz.answer: The nucleus
choices: The nucleus
The cytoplasm
The cell membrane
The vacuole
quiz.explain: In eukaryotic plant and animal cells, the nucleus holds most of the DNA. Bacteria also have DNA but no nucleus; their DNA lies in a nucleoid region.

quiz.prompt: One skeletal-muscle fibre produces only a limited force, yet a whole muscle can lift a heavy bag. How is that possible?
quiz.answer: Many muscle fibres contract together, so their forces add
choices: Each fibre takes a separate turn, so their forces never overlap
Many muscle fibres contract together, so their forces add
The bone stretches the fibres to create extra force
One fibre runs through every muscle in the arm
quiz.explain: A muscle bundles many fibres roughly in parallel, so their coordinated forces add and pull through connective tissue and tendons. Repeating sarcomeres within each fibre shorten together to make the fibre shorten.

quiz.prompt: A single bacterium splits into two every hour. Starting from one bacterium, how many are there after 4 hours?
quiz.explain: Each hour the number doubles: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. Four doublings give 16 cells.

quiz.prompt: A gardener places a thin slice of green leaf tissue and a scraping of frog skin under the same microscope. Which structure can she find in many photosynthetic leaf cells but not in frog skin cells?
quiz.answer: Chloroplasts
choices: A nucleus
Chloroplasts
Watery cytoplasm inside
A membrane around the outside
quiz.explain: Both kinds of cell have membranes and cytoplasm, and typical examples contain nuclei. Chloroplasts capture light in photosynthetic plant cells, but not every plant cell has them: root cells and onion-bulb epidermal cells generally do not.

quiz.prompt: Cheek cells on a slide are nearly invisible until a drop of dye is added, and then their edges show clearly. Why does the dye help?
quiz.answer: It stains some parts darker so the edges stand out
choices: It makes the cells swell up so that they are big enough to see
It kills the cells so they stop drifting about on the slide
It adds extra brightness to the sample beneath the lens
It stains some parts darker so the edges stand out
quiz.explain: Cells are almost transparent, so light passes through them with little to see. A dye is taken up unevenly by different parts, and that difference in darkness is what makes the edges visible.

quiz.prompt: An amoeba in pond water is one single cell, yet it moves about, feeds and grows. What does this show?
quiz.answer: One cell can perform all the core processes of a living organism
choices: Cells can only work once they are joined into tissues
An amoeba must have tiny organs inside it like ours
One cell can perform all the core processes of a living organism
It must really be many cells stuck together
quiz.explain: A single amoeba cell performs core life processes within one cell rather than dividing them among tissues and organs. It still takes in matter and energy from its environment.

nodes.title: Classifying Life
nodes.goal: Kingdoms, species, and the tree of life.

quiz.prompt: A scientist discovers a new creature. To decide how it is related to other living things, biologists mainly group organisms by:
quiz.answer: Shared characteristics and common ancestry
quiz.explain: Classification tries to reflect evolutionary history, so biologists look for features inherited from a shared ancestor. Habitat, diet and general appearance can all be alike in animals that are only distantly related.
choices: How similar they look to one another overall
Shared characteristics and common ancestry
Where each of them lives and how it moves
What each of them eats when fully grown

quiz.prompt: Two animals mate and produce healthy offspring that can also have babies of their own. This tells you they most likely belong to the same:
quiz.answer: Species
quiz.explain: The usual test for one species is that members can breed together and produce fertile offspring. Two breeds of dog can do that, so breed is a division within a species, not a boundary between species.
choices: Species
Breed
Kingdom
Habitat

quiz.prompt: A pond survey finds 4 kinds of insect, 3 kinds of fish and 2 kinds of bird. How many kinds of vertebrate (animals with a backbone) were found?
quiz.explain: Fish and birds have backbones, so 3 + 2 = 5 kinds of vertebrate. Insects have no backbone.

quiz.prompt: A dolphin and a shark both have fins and live in the sea, yet biologists group the dolphin with cows and bats. Why?
quiz.answer: It breathes air and feeds its young milk
choices: It has smooth skin instead of rough scales
It is far more intelligent than any shark
It swims by beating its tail up and down
It breathes air and feeds its young milk
quiz.explain: Lungs and milk are inherited mammal features, shared with cows and bats. Smooth skin, tail movement and intelligence are real differences from a shark, but they are not what places the dolphin among mammals.

quiz.prompt: Which feature is most useful for deciding whether an unfamiliar animal is a bird?
quiz.answer: Feathers
choices: Being able to fly
Having a beak
Laying eggs
Feathers
quiz.explain: Feathers are found on birds and on nothing else alive today. Bats fly, turtles lay eggs and an octopus has a beak, so each of those is shared with animals that are not birds.

quiz.prompt: A mushroom cannot move and pushes up out of the ground, yet biologists do not place it with the plants. What is the main reason?
quiz.answer: It absorbs food made by other organisms
choices: It has no roots reaching down into the soil
It springs up overnight and dies in days
It absorbs food made by other organisms
It has no green colour anywhere in it
quiz.explain: Plants make their own food from light; fungi cannot, and absorb food that something else has made. Lacking roots or green colour are consequences of that difference rather than the reason for it.

quiz.prompt: A field guide lists 24 animals and says 18 of them are invertebrates. How many of the 24 are vertebrates?
quiz.explain: Every animal is either a vertebrate or an invertebrate, so 24 - 18 = 6 vertebrates.

quiz.prompt: Why do scientists give each species a two-word scientific name instead of using everyday names?
quiz.answer: One name works in every language
choices: Everyday names are easier for most people to remember
A scientific name never changes once it has been given
Scientific names are shorter
One name works in every language
quiz.explain: The same animal has different common names in different languages, and one common name can be used for several animals. A single agreed scientific name lets biologists anywhere be certain which species is meant.

quiz.prompt: A bat flies and a robin flies, yet biologists group the bat with mice rather than with birds. Which feature settles it?
quiz.answer: Fur and milk for its young
choices: Fur and milk for its young
Living high up in the trees
A diet made mostly of insects
Wings that it flaps to stay in the air
quiz.explain: Grouping follows ancestry, not lifestyle. Fur and feeding young on milk are mammal features; flight has evolved separately several times.

quiz.prompt: A newt has damp skin with no scales, is cold to the touch, and lays jelly-covered eggs in a pond. Which group fits it best?
quiz.answer: Amphibians
choices: Fish
Amphibians
Winged insects
Reptiles like lizards
quiz.explain: Moist scale-free skin and jelly-covered eggs laid in water are amphibian features. Reptiles have dry scales and lay shelled eggs on land.

lesson_media.alt: A simplified phylogeny branches Bacteria from the shared ancestor and places Eukaryotes within an archaeal host lineage, with a second bacterial contribution to mitochondria.
lesson_media.caption: Classification is nested ancestry, not a ladder: branching marks lineage divergence, while the mitochondrial edge records an endosymbiotic merger.

nodes.title: Photosynthesis
nodes.goal: How plants eat sunlight.

quiz.prompt: During photosynthesis a plant takes in carbon dioxide and water and uses sunlight to make sugar. What gas does it release as a by-product?
quiz.answer: Oxygen
quiz.explain: Photosynthesis releases oxygen as a by-product while producing sugar for the plant.
choices: Carbon dioxide
Oxygen
Hydrogen
Nitrogen

quiz.prompt: A healthy plant is left in a completely dark closet with water and soil for two weeks and becomes weak and pale. What is the best explanation?
quiz.answer: Without light it cannot make its own food
quiz.explain: Light is the energy source for photosynthesis, so in the dark the plant cannot build sugar and must live on what it had stored. Soil supplies minerals and water, never food.
choices: It used up the food that was stored in the soil
It ran out of oxygen in the dark and suffocated
Losing its green colour is what made it weak
Without light it cannot make its own food

quiz.prompt: A plant uses 6 molecules of carbon dioxide to build one sugar molecule. How many carbon dioxide molecules does it need to build 4 sugar molecules?
quiz.explain: Each sugar takes 6 carbon dioxide molecules, so 4 sugars take 6 x 4 = 24.

quiz.prompt: Pondweed in a beaker of water gives off a stream of bubbles under a lamp. When the lamp is moved further away, the bubbling slows down. What is the best explanation?
quiz.answer: Less light reaches the weed, so photosynthesis slows
choices: The water further from the lamp is much colder
Less light reaches the weed, so photosynthesis slows
The pondweed has used up its carbon dioxide
The pondweed rests in dim light and starts again later
quiz.explain: The bubbles are oxygen from photosynthesis; with dimmer light the reaction runs more slowly, so fewer bubbles appear.

quiz.prompt: A tree gains hundreds of kilograms of wood as it grows. Where does most of that added material come from?
quiz.answer: Carbon dioxide taken in from the air
choices: Solid matter taken up through the roots
Water alone, drawn up the trunk
Carbon dioxide taken in from the air
Minerals dissolved in the rain that falls on it
quiz.explain: Most of a tree's dry mass is carbon, and that carbon arrives as carbon dioxide gas from the air, not from the soil.

quiz.prompt: A leaf with green and white patches is left in the light, then tested for starch. Only the green patches turn blue-black. Why?
quiz.answer: The green patches have chlorophyll and can make sugar
choices: The white patches are dead and store no starch
Starch drains out of the paler parts of any leaf
The white patches make sugar but store it as oil
The green patches have chlorophyll and can make sugar
quiz.explain: Chlorophyll is needed to capture light, so only the green regions photosynthesise and store the starch that the test detects.

quiz.prompt: A leaf makes 3 grams of sugar during 8 hours of sunshine. At the same rate, how many grams would it make in 24 hours of that light?
quiz.explain: 24 hours is three lots of 8 hours, so 3 x 3 = 9 grams.

quiz.prompt: Why do gardeners space seedlings apart instead of crowding them all into one patch?
quiz.answer: Crowded leaves shade one another from the light
choices: Crowded plants use up the carbon dioxide around them
Crowded leaves shade one another from the light
Crowded stems tangle and knock each other over
Crowded leaves trap heat and cook one another
quiz.explain: Light is the resource that runs short first when leaves overlap, and a shaded leaf photosynthesises less. Carbon dioxide is replaced constantly by moving air, so it does not run out in an open bed.

quiz.prompt: A plant is given plenty of light and water, but is sealed in a jar from which all the carbon dioxide has been removed. What happens to its sugar making?
quiz.answer: It stops, because one raw material is missing
choices: It carries on, taking carbon from the soil instead
It speeds up, since more light reaches the leaves
It stops, because one raw material is missing
It carries on, using light and water alone
quiz.explain: Sugar is built from carbon dioxide and water using light energy. Remove any one of the three and the reaction cannot run, however plentiful the other two are.

quiz.prompt: In daylight a leaf gives out oxygen, but at night the very same leaf takes oxygen in. Explain how both can be true.
quiz.answer: In the light the leaf photosynthesises and makes far more oxygen than it uses, so oxygen passes out of the leaf. In the dark photosynthesis stops but respiration carries on, so the leaf now takes oxygen in.
quiz.explain: Plants respire all the time. Only in the light does photosynthesis outpace respiration, and that is when a leaf becomes a net source of oxygen.

lesson_media.alt: A leaf flow diagram brings light, six carbon dioxide, and six water molecules into a chloroplast and outputs glucose and six oxygen molecules.
lesson_media.caption: Photosynthesis conserves atoms while changing energy form: carbon dioxide supplies carbon, water supplies electrons, and light drives sugar formation.

nodes.title: Body Systems
nodes.goal: Digestive, circulatory, respiratory, nervous systems.

quiz.prompt: Which body system is mainly responsible for carrying oxygen and nutrients to every cell in the body?
quiz.answer: The circulatory system
quiz.explain: The circulatory system pumps blood, delivering oxygen and nutrients throughout the body.
choices: The respiratory system
The nervous system
The circulatory system
The digestive system

quiz.prompt: You eat a sandwich. Which statement best describes what your digestive system does with it?
quiz.answer: It breaks food into small nutrients the body absorbs
quiz.explain: Digestion breaks large food molecules into pieces small enough to cross the gut wall into the blood. The energy is released later, inside cells, not burned in the stomach.
choices: It removes the waste and lets the rest pass straight on
It burns the food in the stomach to release its energy
It breaks food into small nutrients the body absorbs
It stores the food until the body needs to use it

quiz.prompt: The lining of your small intestine is folded into millions of tiny finger-like villi. Explain how this helps you get what you need from your food.
quiz.answer: The villi give the lining a much bigger surface area, so far more digested nutrients can be absorbed into the blood.
quiz.explain: Folding the lining into villi packs a huge absorbing surface into a short tube, which speeds up how much food can be taken into the blood.

quiz.prompt: Which body system has the main job of getting oxygen out of the air and into the blood?
quiz.answer: The respiratory system
choices: The respiratory system
The circulatory system
The digestive system
The nervous system
quiz.explain: The lungs of the respiratory system bring air close to the blood so oxygen can pass across into it.

quiz.prompt: Muscles can pull, but they cannot push. So how does your arm straighten again after you have bent it?
quiz.answer: A second muscle on the other side pulls it back
choices: The muscle relaxes and the arm drops straight again
The bone springs back into its own straight shape
A second muscle on the other side pulls it back
The bent muscle pushes the bone back outwards
quiz.explain: Muscles work in antagonistic pairs: one pulls the joint one way, and its partner on the opposite side pulls it back. Relaxing alone would let the arm hang, not straighten it against a load.

quiz.prompt: You sprint for a bus. Which pair of systems works together to get extra oxygen to your leg muscles?
quiz.answer: Respiratory and circulatory
choices: Respiratory and circulatory
Digestive and skeletal
Nervous and digestive
Skeletal and respiratory
quiz.explain: The lungs take the oxygen in and the blood carries it to the muscles, so the two systems must work as a pair.

quiz.prompt: A person at rest breathes 20 times a minute. How many breaths is that in half an hour?
quiz.explain: Half an hour is 30 minutes, so 20 x 30 = 600 breaths.

quiz.prompt: Why does chewing food thoroughly help digestion?
quiz.answer: Smaller pieces give the juices more surface to work on
choices: Chewing softens food so the stomach muscles do less work
Smaller pieces give the juices more surface to work on
Chewing warms food so the stomach starts sooner
Smaller pieces are easier to swallow safely
quiz.explain: Digestive enzymes can only act at the surface of a piece of food. Cutting one lump into many small pieces greatly increases the total surface, so digestion goes faster.

quiz.prompt: A patient has a long section of their small intestine removed by surgery. Which problem is most likely afterwards?
quiz.answer: They absorb fewer nutrients from their food
choices: Their stomach must now do all of the absorbing
They can no longer pass waste out of the body
Food is no longer broken down into nutrients
They absorb fewer nutrients from their food
quiz.explain: Almost all absorption happens across the lining of the small intestine, so a shorter intestine means less surface and less taken up. Breaking food down and passing waste out are jobs done elsewhere.

quiz.prompt: The heart is often described as two pumps in one. Explain what that means.
quiz.answer: The right side pumps blood to the lungs to pick up oxygen, and the left side pumps that oxygen-rich blood out around the rest of the body. The two sides drive two separate loops at once.
quiz.explain: Blood makes two circuits: a short one to the lungs and a long one to the body. The two halves of the heart keep them separate so oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor blood do not mix.

lesson_media.alt: A body-systems flow combines absorbed nutrients and inhaled oxygen, then separates carbon dioxide to the lungs, dissolved wastes to the kidneys, and unabsorbed residue to the colon.
lesson_media.caption: Circulation links specialised organs, but different wastes leave by different routes: exhalation, urine formation, and elimination are not one generic process.

nodes.title: Reproduction and Growth
nodes.goal: How living things make more of themselves.

quiz.prompt: A strawberry plant sends out a runner that grows into a new plant identical to the parent. This is an example of:
quiz.answer: Asexual reproduction
quiz.explain: A runner grows a new plant from the parent's own tissue, with one parent and no mixing of instructions, so the offspring is an exact copy. Pollination and seed dispersal are steps in the sexual route instead.
choices: Sexual reproduction, with two parents
Pollination by insects
Asexual reproduction
Seed dispersal

quiz.prompt: A pond is stocked with fish that are well fed and healthy but never breed. Fifty years later there are no fish in the pond. What best explains this?
quiz.answer: Nothing came along to replace the fish as they died
quiz.explain: Every individual dies eventually, so a population lasts only if reproduction replaces the losses. Even in a perfect pond with endless food, a group that never breeds simply runs down to nothing.
choices: The pond water must have turned unsuitable for them
Nothing came along to replace the fish as they died
Fish are unable to live as long as fifty years
The fish must have run out of food in the end

quiz.prompt: A frog lays 200 eggs in a pond. Only 1 in every 20 survives to become an adult frog. How many adult frogs is that?
quiz.explain: 200 divided by 20 gives 10 surviving adults.

quiz.prompt: Puppies in one litter have different coat patterns, but the young plants on a strawberry runner all look identical to the parent. Why the difference?
quiz.answer: Two parents mix instructions; a runner copies one
choices: The puppies grow up in different parts of the garden
Coat pattern is decided by what the puppies are fed
Two parents mix instructions; a runner copies one
A runner grows from a seed the parent drops
quiz.explain: Sexual reproduction shuffles instructions from two parents, so each puppy gets a different combination. A runner is grown from the parent plant's own tissue, so every new plant carries the same instructions.

quiz.prompt: A caterpillar eats leaves while the butterfly it becomes drinks nectar. How does this difference help the species?
quiz.answer: Young and adults never compete for food
choices: Adults need much less food than caterpillars do
Leaves would be too heavy for a flying insect
Nectar is simply easier for an adult to find
Young and adults never compete for food
quiz.explain: When the two stages eat entirely different things, the caterpillars are not taking food from the adults or from each other's stage. The same habitat can then support far more of the species.

quiz.prompt: Why do many plants make seeds with hooks that catch in animal fur?
quiz.answer: The seeds are carried well away from the parent
choices: The animal's fur keeps the seeds warm until spring
The seeds are carried well away from the parent
The hooks stop birds and mice eating the seeds
Hooked seeds sprout faster than smooth ones
quiz.explain: A seed that falls under its parent must compete with it for light and water. Hooking onto a passing animal takes the seed to new ground, which is why so many plants have hooks, wings or tasty fruit.

quiz.prompt: A pair of rabbits has 6 young. When each of those grows up, it too has 6 young. How many rabbits are in that second batch of young?
quiz.explain: Each of the 6 rabbits has 6 young, so 6 x 6 = 36.

quiz.prompt: Bulbs dug from one daffodil clump produce flowers of exactly the same colour year after year. Why?
quiz.answer: Each new bulb is a copy of the same parent plant
choices: Bulbs grow from seeds that keep the parent's colour
Each new bulb is a copy of the same parent plant
The soil the bulbs grow in decides the colour
Bees bring pollen only from the same flower
quiz.explain: New bulbs form from the parent bulb's own tissue, so the whole clump carries identical instructions. Growing daffodils from seed, which mixes two parents, does give flowers that differ.

quiz.prompt: An oak tree makes thousands of acorns each year, while an elephant has a single calf every few years. What best explains the difference?
quiz.answer: Very few acorns ever survive, so a great many must be made
choices: Elephant calves are able to look after themselves from birth
Very few acorns ever survive, so a great many must be made
Oak trees live very much longer lives than elephants do
Acorns grow into full-sized trees within a single year
quiz.explain: An elephant protects and feeds its one calf for years, so most survive. An acorn is left to chance, so the tree makes huge numbers and loses nearly all of them.

quiz.prompt: A cutting from a geranium is stood in water, grows roots and becomes a new plant. Compared with growing one from seed, what is the key difference?
quiz.answer: The new plant matches the parent exactly
choices: The new plant will have a different flower colour
The new plant mixes the features of two parents
The new plant matches the parent exactly
The new plant never flowers
quiz.explain: A cutting is a piece of the parent that has grown roots, so it carries exactly the parent's instructions. A seed comes from two parents and gives a plant that differs from both.

lesson_media.alt: A reproduction network splits into asexual and sexual routes, reconverges at a new organism, and only then proceeds to growth by mitosis and differentiation.
lesson_media.caption: Reproduction establishes a new individual; growth develops that individual, so growth is a later shared process rather than a third reproductive route.

nodes.title: Ecosystems
nodes.goal: Energy flow, food webs, and balance in nature.

quiz.prompt: In a meadow food web, a disease suddenly kills most of the rabbits. What is the most likely immediate effect on the foxes that eat them?
quiz.answer: Fox numbers fall because their food supply has gone
quiz.explain: The foxes depend on the rabbits for food, so losing most of the rabbits removes most of the foxes' supply. More grass helps the rabbits' food supply, which is a step further down the chain.
choices: Fox numbers rise, since the disease has been removed
Fox numbers fall because their food supply has gone
Fox numbers stay level; foxes can live on plants
Fox numbers rise, as more grass is left uneaten

quiz.prompt: Where does the energy that flows through almost every ecosystem originally come from?
quiz.answer: The Sun, captured by producers such as plants
quiz.explain: Producers capture solar energy through photosynthesis, and it then flows to the consumers that eat them.
choices: The soil, eaten directly by grazing animals
Rocks slowly breaking down to release minerals
The predators sitting at the top of the food web
The Sun, captured by producers such as plants

quiz.prompt: In the food chain grass to grasshopper to frog to snake, how many of the four organisms are consumers?
quiz.explain: The grass is the producer; the grasshopper, frog and snake all eat other organisms, so there are 3 consumers.

quiz.prompt: A thick layer of fallen leaves covers a wood in autumn and has almost gone by spring. Which organisms are mainly responsible?
quiz.answer: Decomposers such as fungi and bacteria
choices: Producers such as the grasses and mosses
Predators hunting through the leaf litter
Decomposers such as fungi and bacteria
Rainwater slowly dissolving the leaves away
quiz.explain: Fungi and bacteria feed on dead material, breaking it down and returning its nutrients to the soil.

quiz.prompt: Cats are brought to an island whose ground-nesting birds have never faced a predator. The birds soon disappear. What is the best explanation?
quiz.answer: The birds had no defence at all against a new hunter
choices: The birds had no defence at all against a new hunter
The cats and the birds competed for the same nests
The birds became too frightened to feed at all
The birds flew away to a quieter island
quiz.explain: Traits that protect against predators, such as hiding nests or fleeing, evolve only where predators are present. Birds that have never faced one are easy prey when a hunter arrives.

quiz.prompt: Why does a meadow support far more grass plants than it does foxes?
quiz.answer: Energy is lost at each step up the food chain
choices: Energy is lost at each step up the food chain
Grass is eaten by many animals, so more must grow
Foxes need far more space than a grass plant does
Foxes turn to plants when their prey is scarce
quiz.explain: So less remains. Most of the energy an animal takes in is spent moving, growing and keeping warm, and only a small part is passed on to whatever eats it. Each step up therefore supports far fewer individuals.

quiz.prompt: In a pond, 5 species eat only plants, 3 species eat only other animals, and 2 species eat both. How many of the 10 species eat at least some plant material?
quiz.explain: The 5 plant-only species plus the 2 that eat both makes 7.

quiz.prompt: A pond is netted over so that no water birds can reach it, and frog numbers then climb sharply. What is the best explanation?
quiz.answer: A predator has been kept away
choices: The net stops frogs hopping away to other ponds
Birds had brought in disease
The net keeps the water warmer for the frogs
A predator has been kept away
quiz.explain: Water birds eat frogs and their tadpoles. Shutting the birds out removes that loss, so more of each year's young survive and the population climbs.

quiz.prompt: Why is a food web a better picture of a wood than a single food chain?
quiz.answer: Most animals eat, and are eaten by, several kinds
choices: A web shows which animal in the wood is the strongest
Most animals eat, and are eaten by, several kinds
A web records how many of each animal live there
A food chain misses out the decomposers entirely
quiz.explain: A single chain shows one path through the wood, but a fox eats rabbits, voles and beetles, and each of those is eaten by several predators. A web shows those many links at once, and so shows what happens when one species is lost.

quiz.prompt: A gardener carefully removes every dead leaf and twig from a flower bed each week. Explain why the soil may slowly become poorer over the years.
quiz.answer: Decomposers break dead material down and return its nutrients to the soil. If the dead material is carried away each week, those nutrients never get back into the soil, so the store is not restocked and the plants run short.
quiz.explain: Nutrients cycle: plants take them up, and decomposers release them again from dead matter. Removing the dead matter breaks the loop.

lesson_media.alt: An ecosystem budget separates incoming sunlight from cycling carbon, water, and minerals, then shows heat leaving and nutrients returning after food-web transfers.
lesson_media.caption: Ecosystem balance is dynamic: energy needs continual input while matter is repeatedly reused through producers, consumers, and decomposers.

nodes.title: Tiny Life
nodes.goal: Bacteria, fungi and viruses.

quiz.prompt: Which statement about microbes is correct?
quiz.answer: Some bacteria and fungi are useful, such as yeast
quiz.explain: Most microbes are harmless and many are useful: yeast raises bread, and gut bacteria help digest food. Fungi cannot photosynthesise, and microbes include bacteria and fungi, which are not animals.
choices: All microbes are harmful and cause disease in humans
Fungi make their own food from sunlight like plants
Some bacteria and fungi are useful, such as yeast
Microbes are simply the smallest kind of animal

quiz.prompt: How is a virus different from a bacterium?
quiz.answer: A virus can only reproduce by taking over a living host cell
quiz.explain: A bacterium is a complete cell that can grow and divide on its own. A virus is far smaller, is not a cell, and can copy itself only by taking over a living cell's machinery, which is why antibiotics do not touch it.
choices: A virus can only reproduce by taking over a living host cell
A virus is much larger and more complex than a bacterium
Bacteria need a host cell, while viruses live freely
A virus can be killed by an ordinary antibiotic

quiz.prompt: Bread dough made with yeast rises, but the same dough without yeast stays flat. Explain what the yeast is doing.
quiz.answer: The living yeast feeds on the sugar in the dough and gives off carbon dioxide gas, and the bubbles of gas push the dough up.
quiz.explain: Yeast is a living fungus; as it feeds it releases carbon dioxide, and the trapped bubbles make the dough rise.

quiz.prompt: Why does washing your hands with soap before eating make you less likely to become ill?
quiz.answer: It removes microbes before they reach your mouth
choices: It leaves the hands germ-free for the rest of the day
It removes microbes before they reach your mouth
The hot water, and not the soap, does the work
It kills every microbe on the skin at once
quiz.explain: Soap loosens microbes from the skin so that rinsing carries them away. It does not sterilise the hands, and they pick microbes up again as soon as you touch the next thing.

quiz.prompt: Milk kept in a fridge stays fresh far longer than milk left out on a table. Why?
quiz.answer: Cold slows the microbes that spoil the milk
choices: It is the darkness in the fridge that preserves it
Cold kills the microbes in the milk outright
Cold slows the microbes that spoil the milk
The fridge keeps air away from the milk
quiz.explain: Milk goes off because microbes in it grow and multiply. Cold slows every chemical process in those microbes, so they grow far more slowly, but it does not kill them, which is why cold milk spoils in the end.

quiz.prompt: Which job is really done by the bacteria that live in a healthy human gut?
quiz.answer: They break down food our own enzymes miss
choices: They digest food in the stomach before it moves on
They replace the enzymes the pancreas would make
They are only present when a person is unwell
They break down food our own enzymes miss
quiz.explain: Gut bacteria live mainly in the large intestine and work on fibre and other material our own enzymes cannot handle. They are present in everyone all the time, not only during illness.

quiz.prompt: A single bacterium divides into two every 30 minutes. Starting from one, how many bacteria are there after 3 hours?
quiz.explain: Three hours holds six half-hours, so there are six doublings: 2 to the power 6 is 64.

quiz.prompt: Yoghurt is made by stirring certain bacteria into warm milk. What does this show about bacteria?
quiz.answer: Some are useful to people
choices: Some are useful to people
They are a kind of very small animal
All bacteria make us ill
They can only grow in cold conditions
quiz.explain: Bacteria that sour milk into yoghurt are one of many kinds we depend on, alongside those in cheese, compost and our own gut.

quiz.prompt: A jar of jam that has sat sealed since summer has a furry blue-green patch on the surface. Which microbe is most likely?
quiz.answer: A mould, which is a kind of fungus
choices: Sugar that has crystallised into fuzz
A colony of bacteria on the surface
A mould, which is a kind of fungus
A virus that has fed on the sugar
quiz.explain: A furry, coloured patch is the visible growth of a mould, a fungus that spreads fine threads through the food. Bacteria form flat, slimy films rather than fuzz, and viruses cannot grow outside a living cell.

quiz.prompt: Bread dough rises much better in a warm kitchen than in the fridge. Why does the warm place work better?
quiz.answer: Yeast is a good deal more active when it is warm
choices: Warmth makes the flour grains swell on their own
Yeast is a good deal more active when it is warm
Warm air is lighter and lifts the dough upward
The dough only rises once the yeast has died
quiz.explain: Yeast is alive, and like most living things it works fastest in warmth. Active yeast makes more carbon dioxide, and it is those bubbles trapped in the dough that make it rise.

lesson_media.alt: A true base-ten size axis places a typical virus at 0.1 micrometre, bacterium at 1, and yeast at 10, where the 10-to-100-micrometre animal-cell range begins and overlaps.
lesson_media.caption: Equal spacing means a tenfold size ratio, while the shared 10-micrometre position makes the yeast–animal-cell overlap explicit rather than implying separate size classes.

nodes.title: Genetics
nodes.goal: Genes, inheritance and DNA.

quiz.prompt: In pea plants the allele for purple flowers (P) is dominant over white (p). If you cross two plants that are both Pp, what fraction of the offspring are expected to have white flowers?
quiz.explain: A Pp x Pp cross gives 1 PP : 2 Pp : 1 pp, so only the 1/4 that are pp show the recessive white flowers.

quiz.prompt: A gene is best described as:
quiz.answer: A stretch of DNA that codes for one protein
quiz.explain: A gene is a length of DNA whose base sequence spells out a protein. A chromosome carries thousands of genes, and the protein is the product of a gene rather than the gene itself.
choices: A whole chromosome, one for each inherited trait
The sugar that forms the backbone of an RNA strand
A stretch of DNA that codes for one protein
The protein that the instructions produce

quiz.prompt: A man with a recessive genetic condition (genotype aa) has children with a woman who is a carrier (genotype Aa). What percent of their children are expected to actually have the condition?
quiz.explain: An aa x Aa cross gives half aa (affected) and half Aa (carriers), so 50% are expected to have the condition.

quiz.prompt: Two brown-eyed parents have a blue-eyed child. The blue allele is recessive. What must be true of the parents?
quiz.answer: Each parent carries one hidden blue allele
choices: Each parent carries one hidden blue allele
One of the parents must really have blue eyes
The child's blue allele arose as a new mutation
The blue allele skipped over a whole generation
quiz.explain: A child with the recessive phenotype must have received a recessive allele from each parent, so both parents are heterozygous carriers.

quiz.prompt: Red-green colour blindness is caused by a recessive allele on the X chromosome. Why are many more men affected than women?
quiz.answer: A man has one X, so a single copy shows
choices: A man has one X, so a single copy shows
The allele is carried on the male Y chromosome
A woman's second X repairs the faulty gene
Men inherit a copy from each of their parents
quiz.explain: Men are hemizygous for X-linked genes: with only one X, a single recessive allele is expressed, while a woman needs two.

quiz.prompt: In a bed of red tulips, one plant opens a yellow flower. Explain how a mutation could produce this.
quiz.answer: A mutation changing the DNA of a gene for the red pigment can stop that pigment being made, leaving the underlying yellow colour showing.
quiz.explain: Mutations alter the DNA sequence of a gene; if the altered gene no longer makes a working pigment enzyme, the flower's colour changes.

quiz.prompt: A pea plant with genotype Pp is crossed with one of genotype pp. Out of 200 offspring, how many are expected to have white flowers (pp)?
quiz.explain: A Pp x pp cross gives half Pp and half pp, so 100 of the 200 are expected to be pp and white.

quiz.prompt: A tall pea plant is crossed with a short one, and every single offspring is tall. What does that show about the tall allele?
quiz.answer: It is dominant over the short allele
choices: Short plants cannot pass on their alleles
It is dominant over the short allele
Height is set by the soil rather than by alleles
The offspring took alleles only from the tall parent
quiz.explain: Each offspring received one allele from each parent. If they all look tall, the tall allele masks the short one, which is what dominant means.

quiz.prompt: Two parents of average height have a child who grows much taller than either of them. Which idea explains this best?
quiz.answer: Height depends on many genes that can combine in fresh ways
choices: Height depends on many genes that can combine in fresh ways
A tall grandparent's genes skipped the parents' generation
The child must carry a brand-new mutation of their own
Better food in childhood is the whole explanation
quiz.explain: Height is polygenic: many genes each add a little, so a child can inherit a combination that adds up to more than either parent's. Genes are not skipped, and diet shifts height without explaining this jump.

quiz.prompt: Identical twins carry exactly the same DNA, yet one of them develops far stronger muscles than the other. Explain how that is possible.
quiz.answer: Their genes are identical, but their environment is not: the twin who takes more exercise and eats a different diet builds more muscle. Genes set the range of what is possible and the environment decides where within that range you end up.
quiz.explain: Almost every trait is genes and environment together. Identical twins are the clearest demonstration, because any difference between them must come from outside the DNA.

lesson_media.alt: A genetics flow joins one allele from each parent into a genotype, then connects gene expression to proteins and an environmentally influenced phenotype.
lesson_media.caption: Inheritance transmits DNA variants; development and environment mediate how those variants become observable traits.

nodes.title: Evolution
nodes.goal: Natural selection and the origin of species.

quiz.prompt: A population of beetles lives on dark tree bark. Birds easily spot and eat the lightest beetles. Over many generations, what change is most likely?
quiz.answer: The population becomes darker on average
quiz.explain: Selective predation removes light beetles, so darker individuals survive and pass on their coloring, shifting the population darker.
choices: Each beetle changes its own color to hide
The population becomes lighter on average
Beetles inherit the color of the bark they rest on
The population becomes darker on average

quiz.prompt: Which statement correctly describes natural selection?
quiz.answer: Better-suited individuals survive and leave more offspring
quiz.explain: Selection acts on variation that already exists: individuals whose traits suit the conditions survive and breed more, so those traits become commoner. Nothing is chosen, and there is no direction beyond what fits the conditions.
choices: Individuals choose to evolve new traits during their lives
Better-suited individuals survive and leave more offspring
Members of a species change together at the same time
Evolution pushes organisms steadily toward complexity

quiz.prompt: Bacteria are exposed to an antibiotic. A few happen to carry a mutation that lets them survive it. After treatment, nearly all surviving bacteria are resistant. This is an example of:
quiz.answer: Natural selection favouring the resistant individuals
quiz.explain: The resistant mutations were present before the drug arrived. The antibiotic does not create or teach resistance; it kills everything else, leaving the few already-resistant cells to multiply.
choices: The bacteria adapting their genes during the treatment
The antibiotic teaching the bacteria how to resist it
Natural selection favouring the resistant individuals
Bacteria deciding to become stronger

quiz.prompt: A bacterial population doubles every 30 minutes. Starting from 100 cells, how many cells are there after 2 hours?
quiz.explain: Two hours is four doublings: 100 -> 200 -> 400 -> 800 -> 1600.

quiz.prompt: A human arm, a bat wing and a whale flipper all contain the same arrangement of bones despite doing very different jobs. This pattern is strongest evidence for:
quiz.answer: Descent with modification from a shared ancestor
choices: Each species separately inventing the same design
Descent with modification from a shared ancestor
The three limbs being used for the same task
Animals reshaping their own bones during life
quiz.explain: Homologous structures make sense if an ancestral limb plan was inherited and then modified for different uses in each descendant.

quiz.prompt: Which finding would most weaken the claim that whales evolved from land-living mammals?
quiz.answer: Whale embryos never form hind-limb buds
choices: Whales feed their young on milk, as land mammals do
Fossil whales have been found with small hind legs
Whales breathe air with lungs rather than gills
Whale embryos never form hind-limb buds
quiz.explain: Descent from four-legged ancestors predicts leftover traces of hind limbs. Embryos that never start to form them would remove one of the strongest lines of evidence; milk, lungs and legged fossils all support the claim instead.

quiz.prompt: In a moth population, 20 percent of moths are the dark form. After fifty years of soot-blackened trees, 95 percent are dark. By how many percentage points has the dark form risen?
quiz.explain: 95 - 20 = 75 percentage points.

quiz.prompt: A farmer sprays the same weedkiller on one field year after year, and it gradually stops working. Which account matches natural selection?
quiz.answer: A few weeds already resisted it and left more offspring
choices: The weeds learned to resist it after being sprayed
A few weeds already resisted it and left more offspring
The weedkiller altered the weeds' genes to make them resistant
The weeds passed on resistance they built up during their lives
quiz.explain: Variation comes first and the spray then selects. Resistance is not acquired during a plant's life and cannot be passed on if it were.

quiz.prompt: Fossil horses form a sequence from small many-toed animals to large single-toed ones across tens of millions of years. What does that sequence provide?
quiz.answer: A record of gradual change accumulating over long spans of time
choices: A record of gradual change accumulating over long spans of time
Proof that horses were designed from the start for running
Evidence that species stay just as they are once formed
A complete list of every kind of horse that ever lived
quiz.explain: Fossil sequences show lineages changing over time, though they are always a sample rather than a full record.

quiz.prompt: A peacock's huge tail makes escaping predators harder, yet the trait has spread through the population. Explain how.
quiz.answer: Peahens prefer to mate with the males that have the biggest tails, so those males leave more offspring. The advantage in attracting a mate outweighs the extra risk of being caught, and selection acts on how many offspring survive rather than on survival alone.
quiz.explain: This is sexual selection. What is favoured is whatever raises reproductive success overall, even at some cost to individual survival.

lesson_media.alt: Four linked stages show inherited variation, differential reproductive success, allele-frequency change over generations, and possible lineage divergence.
lesson_media.caption: Natural selection is a population-level consequence of heritable differences in reproductive success, not purposeful improvement within an individual.

nodes.title: Cell Biology
nodes.goal: Organelles, membranes, mitosis.

quiz.prompt: A muscle cell needs a great deal of energy to contract. Which organelle would you expect to find in unusually large numbers inside it?
quiz.answer: Mitochondria
quiz.explain: Mitochondria carry out the reactions that make most of a cell's ATP, so cells with heavy energy demands, such as muscle and heart cells, are packed with them.
choices: The Golgi apparatus
Mitochondria
The nucleus
Ribosomes

quiz.prompt: A human cell with 46 chromosomes divides by mitosis. How many chromosomes will each of the two daughter cells have?
quiz.explain: Mitosis produces two genetically identical daughter cells, each with the same chromosome number as the parent, which is 46.

quiz.prompt: The cell membrane is described as 'selectively permeable.' What does this mean for the cell?
quiz.answer: It lets some substances pass while blocking others
quiz.explain: The membrane admits what the cell needs and holds back what it must keep out or in. That control is what lets the inside of a cell differ from its surroundings.
choices: It blocks everything, so nothing can enter or leave
It lets some substances pass while blocking others
It lets absolutely everything pass through freely
It lets water through but stops everything else

quiz.prompt: A plant cell is placed in a strong salt solution and its contents shrink away from the wall. What has happened?
quiz.answer: Water left the cell by osmosis
choices: The wall shrank and pulled the contents with it
Salt was drawn into the cell and pushed it in
The cell died, and dead contents shrink
Water left the cell by osmosis
quiz.explain: The salt solution is more concentrated than the cell's contents, so water moves out across the membrane. The stiff wall keeps its shape while the shrinking contents pull away from it.

quiz.prompt: Sperm and egg cells are made with half the usual chromosome number. Why does this matter?
quiz.answer: So the fertilised egg is back to normal
choices: So each gamete carries only the genes it needs
So gametes stay small enough to travel easily
So the embryo can double its number quickly
So the fertilised egg is back to normal
quiz.explain: Fertilisation adds two sets together. If each gamete carried the full number, the count would double every generation, so halving it beforehand is what keeps it steady.

quiz.prompt: A mature human red blood cell has no nucleus. Give one advantage of this and one drawback.
quiz.answer: With no nucleus there is more space inside for haemoglobin, so the cell carries more oxygen, but it cannot make new proteins or divide, so it wears out and lives only a few months.
quiz.explain: Losing the nucleus trades long life and repair for carrying capacity, which is why red cells must constantly be replaced by the bone marrow.

quiz.prompt: A cell completes one full cycle of division every 20 hours. Starting from a single cell, how many cells are there after 60 hours?
quiz.explain: Sixty hours allows three divisions, so 1 becomes 2, then 4, then 8.

quiz.prompt: A cell that secretes large amounts of digestive enzyme is unusually packed with ribosomes. Why would you expect that?
quiz.answer: Ribosomes make the proteins, and enzymes are proteins
choices: Ribosomes make the proteins, and enzymes are proteins
Ribosomes wrap the enzyme into vesicles for export
Ribosomes supply the energy that secretion needs
Ribosomes store the enzyme until it is needed
quiz.explain: Ribosomes are where amino acids are joined into protein chains. A cell exporting large amounts of a protein enzyme needs many of them, while packaging is the Golgi's job and energy comes from mitochondria.

quiz.prompt: Placed in pure water, an onion cell swells but holds together, while a red blood cell bursts. What accounts for the difference?
quiz.answer: The plant cell wall resists the pressure
choices: The onion cell's membrane is far stronger than a blood cell's
The onion cell's vacuole soaks up the extra water
The plant cell wall resists the pressure
Blood cells take in water much faster
quiz.explain: Both cells take in water and swell. The plant cell is held by a rigid cellulose wall that pushes back once it is full, while the red blood cell has only a membrane and bursts.

quiz.prompt: A drug stops spindle fibres forming just as a cell enters mitosis. What is the most likely result?
quiz.answer: Chromosomes are not pulled apart, so the counts go wrong
choices: The membrane fails to pinch in, giving one cell with two nuclei
Chromosomes are not pulled apart, so the counts go wrong
The chromosomes never condense, so nothing shows
The DNA is never copied in the first place
quiz.explain: Spindle fibres attach to the chromosomes and drag one copy of each to either end. Without them the copies are not separated, so the daughter cells receive the wrong numbers; copying and condensing have already happened.

lesson_media.alt: A cell network links selective membrane exchange and nuclear DNA to ribosome-made proteins, mitochondrial ATP, and coordinated cell work.
lesson_media.caption: Organelles divide labour but remain coupled by flows of information, matter, and energy; mitosis preserves the genome during cell division.

nodes.title: Human Anatomy & Physiology
