nodes.goal: How human organs are organized and how major body systems coordinate circulation, gas exchange, control and waste removal.

lesson_media.alt: Separate teaching specimens show a cutaway heart, a pair of lungs and a standing body with major vessels; each is presented on its own rather than as a connected circulation route.
lesson_media.caption: These separate teaching specimens frame the heart, lungs and whole body; they are not a connected route diagram. Use the model to trace an ordered schematic of blood's cardiopulmonary path.

lesson_media.title: Trace the circulation route
lesson_media.instructions: Advance through the cardiopulmonary circuit from body tissues to the right heart, lungs, left heart and back to the body. Use the oxygenation cues to distinguish blood returning from the body from blood returning from the lungs.

quiz.prompt: You touch a hot stove and your hand begins to withdraw before you consciously feel the pain. Which pathway initiates this rapid response?
quiz.answer: A reflex arc carried by nerves to and from the spinal cord
quiz.explain: Sensory neurons enter the spinal cord, where interneurons activate motor neurons and can begin the withdrawal without waiting for conscious processing. At the same time, ascending pathways carry signals to the brain, where the pain becomes consciously perceived.
choices: A reflex arc carried by nerves to and from the spinal cord
A signal that goes to the brain and back before you move
A slow chemical message sent through the bloodstream
A muscle acting on its own without any signal

quiz.prompt: In the lungs, oxygen moves from the air in the alveoli into the blood. What drives this movement?
quiz.answer: Diffusion down an oxygen partial-pressure gradient
quiz.explain: The partial pressure of oxygen is higher in alveolar gas than in the deoxygenated blood arriving in the lung capillaries, so oxygen diffuses across the thin alveolar-capillary barrier down that gradient. Ventilation and blood flow help maintain the gradient; no active pump is required.
choices: Active pumping by the alveoli that uses cell energy
Gravity pulling the heavier oxygen down into blood
The blood's suction pulls oxygen out of the air
Diffusion down an oxygen partial-pressure gradient

quiz.prompt: When you exercise hard, both your heart rate and breathing rate increase. What is the main purpose of these changes?
quiz.answer: To bring the muscles more oxygen and clear carbon dioxide
quiz.explain: Working muscles use oxygen faster and produce carbon dioxide faster. Breathing harder loads more oxygen and unloads more carbon dioxide, and a faster heart delivers and collects it more quickly.
choices: To push more blood into the muscles to make them bigger
To bring the muscles more oxygen and clear carbon dioxide
To replace the oxygen used up by the brain in thinking
To warm the muscles up so they work more smoothly

quiz.prompt: A resting heart beats 72 times a minute and pushes out 70 mL of blood with each beat. What is the cardiac output in millilitres per minute?
quiz.explain: Cardiac output is heart rate times stroke volume: 72 x 70 = 5040 mL per minute.

quiz.prompt: Blood returning from the body enters the right side of the heart. Where is it pumped next?
quiz.answer: To the lungs
choices: To the lungs
To the brain
To the liver
Around the whole body
quiz.explain: The right side sends blood to the lungs to pick up oxygen; the left side then pumps that oxygenated blood around the body.

quiz.prompt: A patient's kidneys stop filtering the blood. Which change would you expect to see in a blood test?
quiz.answer: Urea builds up in the blood
choices: Water and salt levels stay exactly right
Glucose vanishes from the blood entirely
Blood oxygen rises sharply
Urea builds up in the blood
quiz.explain: The kidneys remove urea, the waste left from breaking down protein. If they stop filtering, urea accumulates in the blood, and water and salt balance drifts too rather than staying right.

quiz.prompt: A person's tidal volume is 500 mL, and 150 mL of each breath stays in the airways without reaching the alveoli. How many millilitres of fresh air reach the alveoli per breath?
quiz.explain: 500 - 150 = 350 mL of each breath reaches the gas-exchange surfaces.

quiz.prompt: Arteries generally have thick, muscular, elastic walls. Many veins, especially those in the limbs, have thinner walls and one-way valves. What best explains these differences?
quiz.answer: Arteries carry blood at high pressure; veins return it at low
choices: Arteries carry blood at high pressure; veins return it at low
Veins lie further from the heart, so face less strain
Arteries carry oxygen-rich blood and veins never do
Veins carry less blood than arteries do
quiz.explain: Each heartbeat drives blood into the arteries at relatively high pressure, so their walls are thick and elastic. Venous pressure is lower; many limb veins use valves together with muscle contractions to limit backflow, although not all veins contain valves.

quiz.prompt: Someone standing still in a hot room faints, and lying them flat helps within seconds. Why does that help so quickly?
quiz.answer: It improves venous return and cerebral perfusion by reducing the hydrostatic gradient
choices: The heart beats more slowly and saves its strength
More air reaches the lungs when the chest is flat
It improves venous return and cerebral perfusion by reducing the hydrostatic gradient
Lying down lets the body cool much faster
quiz.explain: Heat and prolonged standing promote blood pooling in the legs, reducing venous return, cardiac output and cerebral perfusion. Lying flat reduces the gravitational hydrostatic gradient between the heart and brain and helps pooled blood return to the chest, restoring cerebral perfusion.

quiz.prompt: Explain why someone whose leg vein valves have been damaged tends to get swollen ankles.
quiz.answer: The valves normally stop blood draining backwards down the leg. When they fail, blood pools in the lower leg, the pressure inside the vessels rises, and fluid is pushed out into the surrounding tissue, which swells.
quiz.explain: Venous return depends on valves plus the squeeze of leg muscles. Losing the valves raises capillary pressure, and swelling follows.

nodes.title: Ecology
nodes.goal: Populations, communities, and cycles of matter.

quiz.prompt: A farmer plants clover, which hosts nitrogen-fixing bacteria in its roots, to improve poor soil. How does this help?
quiz.answer: Bacteria convert nitrogen gas into a form plants can use
quiz.explain: Air is four-fifths nitrogen, but plants cannot use the gas. Bacteria in clover root nodules fix it into ammonium, which the clover uses and which enriches the soil when the plant dies back.
choices: Bacteria convert nitrogen gas into a form plants can use
The clover's deep roots bring nitrogen up from below
The clover simply blocks the sunlight that weeds need
The bacteria strip the nitrogen out of the soil

quiz.prompt: A deer population grows rapidly, then levels off near the maximum number the land can support. This upper limit is called the:
quiz.answer: Carrying capacity
quiz.explain: Carrying capacity is the maximum population size an environment can sustain given its available resources.
choices: Carrying capacity
Population density
Trophic efficiency
Biotic potential

quiz.prompt: Both burning fossil fuels and cutting down forests raise atmospheric carbon dioxide. Why does deforestation contribute to the rise?
quiz.answer: Fewer trees remain to absorb carbon dioxide from the air
quiz.explain: Growing trees take carbon dioxide out of the air and lock the carbon into wood. Removing them removes that withdrawal, and burning or rotting the felled wood returns its carbon as well.
choices: Trees give out oxygen, which destroys the carbon dioxide
Fewer trees remain to absorb carbon dioxide from the air
Cleared ground reflects more sunlight back into space
Tree roots pump carbon dioxide down into the soil

quiz.prompt: Producers in a field capture 20,000 kJ of energy. About 10% passes on at each step. How many kJ reach the secondary consumers (two steps up)?
quiz.explain: 10% of 20,000 is 2,000 for the primary consumers, and 10% of that is 200 kJ for the secondary consumers.

quiz.prompt: When sea otters are removed from a coast, sea urchins multiply and strip away the kelp forest, and the whole community changes. What does this show about the otter?
quiz.answer: It is a keystone species in this community
choices: It competes with the kelp for the same nutrients
It is a producer at the base of this food web
It is the most numerous animal on that coast
It is a keystone species in this community
quiz.explain: A keystone species has an effect on the community far out of proportion to its numbers. By eating urchins the otter protects the kelp forest that everything else depends on, so removing it changes the whole system.

quiz.prompt: A farmer sprays insecticide on a field. Explain why the number of birds of prey nearby may fall as a result.
quiz.answer: The insecticide kills the insects that small birds eat, and the chemical also becomes more concentrated as it passes up the food chain, so predators are left with less prey and a higher dose.
quiz.explain: Pesticides act both by removing prey and by bioaccumulating, so top predators suffer most even though they were never sprayed.

quiz.prompt: A lake holds 800 fish. Each year 25 percent of the fish present are caught, and none breed. How many fish remain after 2 years?
quiz.explain: After one year 800 x 0.75 = 600 remain; after two, 600 x 0.75 = 450.

quiz.prompt: A lake beside heavily fertilised fields turns green, and weeks later the fish die. What is the best account?
quiz.answer: Nutrients feed an algal bloom whose decay uses up the oxygen
choices: Nutrients feed an algal bloom whose decay uses up the oxygen
The fertiliser makes the water too salty for the fish
The fertiliser poisons the fish through their gills
The green colour stops the fish from finding food
quiz.explain: Fertiliser runoff supplies the nutrients algae need, so they bloom and turn the water green. When the bloom dies, the bacteria decomposing it consume the dissolved oxygen, and the fish suffocate weeks after the fertiliser arrived.

quiz.prompt: Two bird species on one island eat the same seeds. Over generations one shifts to feeding on larger seeds. What does this illustrate?
quiz.answer: Competition pushing the two species apart in what they use
choices: Competition pushing the two species apart in what they use
Mutualism, in which both species gain from the other
Random drift, with no ecological cause at all
Predation, which is holding one population down
quiz.explain: While both species take the same seeds, each one reduces the other's supply. Individuals that specialise on a size the other neglects face less competition and leave more offspring, so the two diverge.

quiz.prompt: Nitrogen makes up most of the air, yet crops are often short of nitrogen. Why?
quiz.answer: Plants are unable to use nitrogen gas directly
choices: Nitrogen is used up by the plant faster than any other
Air does not reach a plant's roots in the soil
Plants are unable to use nitrogen gas directly
Nitrogen gas is too large to enter a leaf
quiz.explain: The two atoms in nitrogen gas are held by a very strong triple bond, and plants have no way of breaking it. They take nitrogen up from the soil as nitrate or ammonium, which bacteria or lightning must make first.

lesson_media.alt: A carbon network sends atmospheric carbon dioxide into producers by photosynthesis and returns it through plant, animal, and decomposer respiration, with feeding and remains linking the living pools.
lesson_media.caption: Carbon follows several simultaneous fluxes rather than one loop: every living group respires, while only carbon-fixing producers drive the major atmospheric input shown.

nodes.title: Microbiology & Disease
nodes.goal: Germs, immunity and vaccines.

quiz.prompt: How does a vaccine protect you from a disease before you are ever exposed to it?
quiz.answer: It trains the immune system to recognise that pathogen early
quiz.explain: A vaccine shows the immune system a harmless version of the pathogen's surface, so memory cells are made in advance. If the real pathogen arrives, the response is fast enough to stop illness developing.
choices: It trains the immune system to recognise that pathogen early
It supplies ready-made antibodies that last for life
It strengthens the skin barrier against the pathogen
It kills any of that pathogen already in the body

quiz.prompt: A doctor refuses to prescribe antibiotics for a patient's common cold. What is the best scientific reason?
quiz.answer: Colds are caused by viruses, and antibiotics do not kill them
quiz.explain: Antibiotics attack structures and processes that only bacteria have, such as the cell wall. A virus has none of them, so the drug cannot work here whatever else might also be true of overuse.
choices: Overuse would breed resistance in this patient's cold virus
Colds are caused by viruses, and antibiotics do not kill them
Antibiotics would kill the useful gut bacteria too
The cold is not yet serious enough to treat

quiz.prompt: A person who recovers from chickenpox rarely catches it again. Which part of the immune system is mainly responsible for this long-term protection?
quiz.answer: Memory cells that remember the pathogen
quiz.explain: After an infection a population of long-lived memory lymphocytes remains. They respond far faster and more strongly on a second encounter, so the pathogen is cleared before symptoms appear.
choices: Skin that has become resistant where the rash was
Antibodies that keep circulating for a lifetime
White cells that engulf any microbe they meet
Memory cells that remember the pathogen

quiz.prompt: A bacterial culture doubles every 20 minutes. Starting from a single cell, how many cells are there after 2 hours?
quiz.explain: Two hours allows six doublings, and 2 to the power 6 is 64.

quiz.prompt: Two antibiotic discs are placed on a lawn of one bacterial strain. Disc A leaves a clear zone 8 mm across; disc B leaves one 20 mm across. What is the best conclusion?
quiz.answer: Antibiotic B is more effective against this bacterium
choices: Antibiotic A kills more slowly but just as completely
Antibiotic B is more effective against this bacterium
Antibiotic B must be effective against every strain
Antibiotic A is the safer choice for a patient
quiz.explain: The clear zone is where bacteria could not grow as the antibiotic diffused outwards, so a wider zone means the drug stopped growth at lower concentrations. That says nothing about safety, or about any other strain.

quiz.prompt: Why should a course of antibiotics be finished even after the patient feels better?
quiz.answer: The bacteria still alive at that point are the hardest to kill
choices: The bacteria still alive at that point are the hardest to kill
The drug only reaches full strength in the second week
The body would become resistant to the drug itself
Feeling better means the infection has fully gone
quiz.explain: The most susceptible bacteria die first, which is why symptoms ease early. Stopping then leaves the toughest survivors to multiply, and it is the bacteria, not the patient, that become resistant.

quiz.prompt: In a trial, 400 vaccinated people and 400 unvaccinated people are exposed. 8 vaccinated and 96 unvaccinated fall ill. How many times higher is the illness rate in the unvaccinated group?
quiz.explain: Both groups are the same size, so compare the counts directly: 96 divided by 8 is 12.

quiz.prompt: Why must a flu vaccine be renewed most years, while a measles vaccine lasts decades?
quiz.answer: Flu's surface proteins change fast
choices: Flu's surface proteins change fast
Flu infects the lungs, where memory cells cannot reach
Immunity to flu is never as strong as to measles
The flu vaccine simply wears off
quiz.explain: So old memory fits poorly. Memory cells recognise a particular surface shape. Influenza changes those surface proteins from year to year, so last year's memory matches badly, while measles surfaces barely change and one exposure lasts decades.

quiz.prompt: A hospital requires staff to wash their hands between patients even when gloves have been worn. What is the main reasoning?
quiz.answer: Hands pick up microbes as the gloves go on and off
choices: Washing is required by law, whatever gloves are worn
Gloves stop protecting after a few minutes of wear
Hands pick up microbes as the gloves go on and off
Some microbes pass straight through latex gloves
quiz.explain: Hands are contaminated as gloves are pulled off, since the outside of a used glove touches the skin, and again from the gloves' outer surface as fresh ones go on. Washing between patients closes that route.

quiz.prompt: During an infection the body deliberately raises its own temperature. What is the likeliest benefit?
quiz.answer: Heat slows pathogens and speeds immune responses
choices: A high temperature stops any pathogen entering a cell
Heat makes white cells multiply almost instantly
Heat slows pathogens and speeds immune responses
Fever is a side effect with no benefit at all
quiz.explain: Many bacteria and viruses replicate best at normal body temperature, so a few degrees hinders them, while most immune reactions run faster when warm. Fever is a controlled response, not an accident.

lesson_media.alt: A time-ordered infection diagram moves from pathogen exposure through innate defence and specific adaptive expansion to long-lived immune memory.
lesson_media.caption: Innate immunity acts quickly and broadly; adaptive immunity takes time to select and multiply matching cells, then preserves a faster memory response.

nodes.title: Botany
nodes.goal: Plant structure, function and diversity.

quiz.prompt: Water absorbed by a plant's roots must reach the leaves at the top. Which tissue transports it upward?
quiz.answer: Xylem
quiz.explain: Xylem is a chain of hollow, reinforced tubes running from root to leaf, carrying water and dissolved minerals upward. Phloem carries sugar in both directions, and the cuticle and stomata sit on the leaf surface.
choices: The waxy cuticle
The stomata
Phloem
Xylem

quiz.prompt: On a very hot, dry day, many plants close the tiny pores (stomata) on their leaves. What is the main benefit of doing this?
quiz.answer: It cuts water loss by evaporation
quiz.explain: Most water lost by a plant escapes as vapour through open stomata. Closing them saves water at the cost of shutting out carbon dioxide, so photosynthesis slows, which is the trade the plant accepts on a hot day.
choices: It stops the leaf from overheating in the sun
It speeds up photosynthesis in the leaf
It lets in much more carbon dioxide
It cuts water loss by evaporation

quiz.prompt: Flowering plants often produce colorful, scented flowers. In terms of reproduction, what is the main purpose of these features?
quiz.answer: To attract pollinators that carry pollen away
quiz.explain: Colour and scent advertise nectar to insects and birds, which pick up pollen at one flower and deliver it to another. Leaves, not petals, capture light, and seed dispersal is advertised later by fruit.
choices: To warn insects away from the seeds as they grow
To attract pollinators that carry pollen away
To catch extra sunlight for making more food
To attract animals that will eat the seeds

quiz.prompt: A potted plant loses 1.5 g of water per hour by transpiration. How many grams does it lose in 8 hours?
quiz.explain: 1.5 g per hour for 8 hours gives 1.5 x 8 = 12 g.

quiz.prompt: A ring of bark is cut away all round a tree trunk. The leaves stay green for weeks, but the roots die and then the tree dies. What does this suggest?
quiz.answer: Sugar can no longer travel down to the roots
choices: The tree loses its water through the cut ring
Sugar can no longer travel down to the roots
The roots are starved of oxygen by the cut
Water can no longer rise up from the roots
quiz.explain: The phloem, which carries sugar from the leaves, lies just inside the bark and is cut away with it; the xylem lies deeper and still carries water up, which is why the leaves stay green. The roots starve first, and the tree follows.

quiz.prompt: A seedling on a windowsill bends towards the glass. What is happening in the stem?
quiz.answer: Cells on the shaded side grow much longer
choices: Cells on the lit side of the stem grow faster
The lit side dries out and shrinks a little
Cells on the shaded side grow much longer
The lit side stops growing altogether
quiz.explain: Auxin accumulates on the shaded side and makes those cells elongate more than the cells facing the light. One side growing longer than the other tips the stem over towards the window.

quiz.prompt: A leaf carries about 300 stomata per square millimetre of its lower surface. How many stomata are there on 20 square millimetres of that surface?
quiz.explain: 300 x 20 = 6,000 stomata.

quiz.prompt: Seedlings are grown in the dark on a slowly rotating drum, so gravity pulls from every direction in turn. Their roots grow straight out instead of downward. What does this suggest?
quiz.answer: Roots normally use a steady pull of gravity as a direction cue
choices: Roots grow downward only when they sense water below
Roots normally use a steady pull of gravity as a direction cue
Roots simply follow the direction the seed was planted
Movement of any kind makes roots grow straight
quiz.explain: Removing a constant gravity direction removes the cue, and the growth response disappears with it.

quiz.prompt: Mosses stay a few centimetres tall and cling to damp places, while ferns and trees grow far taller. Which difference explains this best?
quiz.answer: Mosses lack the vessels that lift water upward
choices: Moss cells are far smaller than the cells of a tree
Mosses lack the vessels that lift water upward
Mosses simply grow too slowly to become tall
Mosses have no roots to anchor a tall stem
quiz.explain: Ferns and trees have xylem, a plumbing system that carries water metres upward and stiffens the stem as well. A moss has neither, so it must stay short enough for water to move cell by cell and damp enough not to dry out.

quiz.prompt: A cut flower left out of water wilts, but often recovers if it is put back into water quickly. Explain both parts.
quiz.answer: Water keeps leaving the leaves by transpiration. With no supply, the cells lose water and their turgor pressure, so the stem goes limp. Standing it back in water lets the cells take water up again by osmosis and become turgid, and the stem stiffens.
quiz.explain: Non-woody plants are held up by water pressure inside their cells, which is why wilting is reversible until the cells are damaged.

lesson_media.alt: A vascular plant diagram joins root water uptake and leaf carbon dioxide capture to xylem transpiration and phloem sugar delivery to sinks.
lesson_media.caption: Plant function emerges from a constrained exchange: stomata must admit carbon dioxide while limiting water loss, and vascular tissues connect distant organs.

nodes.title: Molecular Biology
nodes.goal: Transcription, translation, gene regulation.

lesson_media.alt: Three panels show DNA transcribed to one RNA strand in a nucleus, that RNA exported through a nuclear pore, and a cytoplasmic ribosome using transfer RNAs to assemble a short peptide.
lesson_media.caption: In a eukaryotic cell, transcription produces RNA in the nucleus, export moves a processed messenger RNA to the cytoplasm, and a ribosome translates its codons into a polypeptide.

lesson_media.title: Step through gene expression
lesson_media.instructions: Switch the example gene on, then transcribe, export and translate its fixed coding sequence one stage at a time. Track which molecule exists in which compartment.

quiz.prompt: The usual flow of sequence information for protein synthesis is DNA to RNA to protein. A drug degrades all messenger RNA in a cell while leaving its DNA and ribosomes intact. What do you predict?
quiz.answer: New protein synthesis stops until fresh mRNA is transcribed
quiz.explain: Ribosomes translate mRNA rather than reading chromosomal DNA directly, so new translation halts until transcripts are replaced. Proteins already made persist according to their half-lives. Reverse transcription can copy RNA into DNA, but sequence information is not copied from protein back into nucleic acid.
choices: Ribosomes switch to reading the DNA template directly
New protein synthesis stops until fresh mRNA is transcribed
Proteins already in the cell are destroyed along with it
The cell copies protein back into RNA to replace the loss

quiz.prompt: In the genetic code, a sequence of three RNA bases (a codon) specifies one amino acid. A messenger RNA has 30 coding bases, not counting the stop codon. How many amino acids will the resulting protein chain contain?
quiz.explain: Each codon is three bases, so 30 divided by 3 gives 10 amino acids.

quiz.prompt: Nearly every cell in your body contains the same DNA, yet a liver cell and a neuron look and behave very differently. What best explains this?
quiz.answer: Different sets of genes are switched on and off in each cell type
quiz.explain: Cell identity arises from differential gene regulation, with each cell type expressing a distinct subset of the shared genome.
choices: Neurons lose most of their own DNA during development
Different sets of genes are switched on and off in each cell type
The DNA sequence mutates differently in each cell type
Liver cells and neurons contain entirely different genomes

quiz.prompt: A single base change turns the codon UGG, which specifies tryptophan, into UGA. What effect on the protein product would you predict?
quiz.answer: Translation stops early, giving a shortened protein
choices: One amino acid is swapped for a chemically similar one
Translation stops early, giving a shortened protein
An extra amino acid is inserted at that position
Every later codon is read in a shifted frame
quiz.explain: UGA is a stop codon, so the ribosome releases the chain there. Substituting one base for another does not shift the frame or add a residue, and the truncated protein usually loses its function.

quiz.prompt: Deleting the repressor gene of a bacterial inducible operon makes the operon's enzymes appear even when no inducer is present. What does that result establish?
quiz.answer: The repressor normally blocks transcription in the uninduced state
choices: The repressor is what switches transcription on directly
The repressor normally blocks transcription in the uninduced state
The inducer must activate the promoter directly
The enzymes are unstable unless the inducer is there to protect them
quiz.explain: Deleting the gene and observing constitutive expression supports the repressor's role as a negative regulator in the uninduced state. This result alone does not establish that the inducer binds the repressor directly; that molecular interaction needs separate evidence.

quiz.prompt: Cells infected with a retrovirus stop producing new viral genomes when treated with a drug that inhibits reverse transcriptase. Explain what reverse transcriptase normally does.
quiz.answer: It builds a DNA copy from the viral RNA template, the step a retrovirus needs before its genome can be integrated into the host chromosome and replicated.
quiz.explain: Reverse transcriptase copies RNA into DNA, reversing the common direction of transcription but not violating the central dogma's prohibition on transferring sequence information from protein back to nucleic acid. Blocking it interrupts the retroviral replication cycle.

quiz.prompt: A gene's coding sequence is 1,203 bases long, counting the stop codon. How many amino acids are in the finished polypeptide?
quiz.explain: 1,203 divided by 3 gives 401 codons; one of these is the stop codon, which specifies no amino acid, leaving 400.

quiz.prompt: A splice-site mutation causes one internal protein-coding exon to be skipped. The exon begins and ends in compatible codon phases and its length is a multiple of three. Which prediction best follows, assuming translation still initiates normally?
quiz.answer: The reading frame is preserved, but the protein lacks that exon's residues
choices: The gene can no longer be transcribed at all
The reading frame is preserved, but the protein lacks that exon's residues
The mutation has no effect, since introns are removed anyway
Translation starts instead from a downstream start codon
quiz.explain: With an internal coding exon, compatible splice phases and a length divisible by three, joining the neighboring exons preserves the downstream reading frame. The protein lacks those residues and may still misfold or lose function; frame preservation does not make the deletion harmless.

quiz.prompt: A strong promoter is swapped in ahead of a weakly expressed bacterial gene. mRNA rises tenfold, but the protein rises a hundredfold. What does the mismatch most suggest?
quiz.answer: Something also raises translation rate or protein stability
choices: The mRNA measurement must have been made too early
Something also raises translation rate or protein stability
The new promoter must also be making the mRNA far more stable
The promoter swap did not actually work
quiz.explain: Protein level is mRNA level multiplied by output per mRNA. A bigger protein change than mRNA change means the per-mRNA term moved too. Extra mRNA stability would already show up in the measured mRNA level, so it cannot be the explanation.

quiz.prompt: Cells are given a drug that blocks RNA polymerase. One protein's level collapses within minutes; another barely shifts over several hours. What best explains the contrast?
quiz.answer: Their mRNAs and/or proteins have very different half-lives
choices: The collapsing protein's gene is far more sensitive to the drug
Their mRNAs and/or proteins have very different half-lives
The stable protein is transcribed much more often than the other
Only the collapsing protein depends on RNA polymerase at all
quiz.explain: Blocking transcription reveals persistence across two stages. Existing mRNA can continue to be translated until it decays, and existing protein persists until it is degraded, so differences in either mRNA half-life or protein half-life can produce the contrast.

nodes.title: Biochemistry
nodes.goal: Proteins, enzymes, metabolism.

quiz.prompt: A reaction that would take days in a warm tube finishes in seconds once its enzyme is added, and the enzyme is recovered unchanged afterwards. What has the enzyme done?
quiz.answer: Lowered the activation energy that the reaction must cross first
quiz.explain: Enzymes lower the activation barrier, which speeds the forward and reverse rates by the same factor. They add no energy, change neither the energy released nor the equilibrium position, and emerge unchanged.
choices: Raised the temperature at the active site enough to drive it
Lowered the activation energy that the reaction must cross first
Made the reaction release more energy than it otherwise would
Shifted the reaction's equilibrium towards the products

quiz.prompt: A digestive enzyme works best at body temperature and pH 7. Placed in a very acidic solution at pH 2, its activity drops sharply. The most likely reason is:
quiz.answer: The low pH distorts the enzyme's fold and so its active site too
quiz.explain: Enzyme activity depends on a precise three-dimensional fold held together by charged and hydrogen-bonded contacts. A pH far from the optimum changes those charges and denatures the protein, so the active site no longer matches the substrate.
choices: The acid breaks the substrate down before the enzyme can act
The low pH distorts the enzyme's fold and so its active site too
Hydrogen ions coat the substrate so that it no longer fits
The enzyme is used up faster in acid than at neutral pH

quiz.prompt: A muscle cell's whole store of ATP would power a hard sprint for only a couple of seconds, yet a sprint lasts far longer than that. What must be true?
quiz.answer: ATP is regenerated from ADP as fast as contraction spends it
quiz.explain: ATP is a turnover currency rather than a store. The pool is small and is recycled many times a minute, with respiration rebuilding ATP from ADP as fast as contraction spends it.
choices: Muscle stores enough extra ATP in the mitochondria to cover it
ATP is regenerated from ADP as fast as contraction spends it
Glucose powers the contraction directly, without ATP
The energy comes from heat released by the working muscle

quiz.prompt: Complete aerobic oxidation of one glucose molecule yields about 30 ATP, while anaerobic glycolysis alone yields 2. How many times more ATP does the aerobic route give?
quiz.explain: 30 divided by 2 is 15 times as much ATP per glucose.

quiz.prompt: A competitive inhibitor occupies an enzyme's active site, so inhibitor and substrate compete for the same place. A tube holding the enzyme and the inhibitor is flooded with a large excess of substrate. What happens to the rate?
quiz.answer: It returns to the normal maximum rate
choices: It stays depressed, because the inhibitor is still there
It returns to the normal maximum rate
It climbs above the usual maximum
It falls further as more inhibited complex forms
quiz.explain: Competition is settled by relative concentration, so enough substrate outbids the inhibitor for the active site and Vmax is reached after all. What the inhibitor changes is the substrate concentration needed to get halfway there, which is why the apparent Km rises.

quiz.prompt: Cyanide blocks the final electron acceptor of the mitochondrial electron transport chain. What follows most directly inside the mitochondrion?
quiz.answer: The proton gradient collapses and ATP output stops
choices: Glycolysis in the cytoplasm halts at the same instant
The proton gradient collapses and ATP output stops
The cell switches to burning fat, so ATP output is unchanged
The Krebs cycle speeds up to cover the shortfall
quiz.explain: With electrons unable to reach oxygen, proton pumping ceases and the gradient dissipates, so ATP synthase stops turning. The Krebs cycle then stalls as NAD+ runs out; only glycolysis continues, and burning fat needs the same chain.

quiz.prompt: An enzyme has a Km of 4 mM. When the substrate concentration is exactly 4 mM, what percentage of Vmax is the reaction rate?
quiz.explain: By definition Km is the substrate concentration giving half the maximum rate, so the rate is 50 percent of Vmax.

quiz.prompt: An enzyme has Vmax = 60 micromoles per minute and Km = 2 mM. Using v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]), give the rate in micromoles per minute at a substrate concentration of 6 mM.
quiz.explain: v = 60 x 6 / (2 + 6) = 360 / 8 = 45 micromoles per minute.

quiz.prompt: An inhibitor lowers an enzyme's apparent Vmax and its apparent Km by the same factor, and adding more substrate makes matters worse rather than better. Which class fits?
quiz.answer: An inhibitor that binds only the enzyme-substrate complex, never free enzyme
choices: A competitive inhibitor, outcompeted by extra substrate
An inhibitor that binds only the enzyme-substrate complex, never free enzyme
A non-competitive inhibitor binding enzyme and complex alike
A partial inhibitor that slows every catalytic cycle equally
quiz.explain: An inhibitor that needs substrate already bound gets more, not less, effective as substrate rises. Trapping enzyme in the inhibited complex also pulls the binding equilibrium forward, which is why apparent Vmax and Km fall by the same factor.

quiz.prompt: A chemical makes the inner mitochondrial membrane freely permeable to protons. What do you predict for a cell exposed to it?
quiz.answer: Fuel is burned faster and the energy escapes as heat
choices: ATP yield per glucose rises, as protons flow more freely
Oxygen use falls, since the chain has nothing to drive
Fuel is burned faster and the energy escapes as heat
Glycolysis halts because ATP has become plentiful
quiz.explain: Uncoupling separates electron transport from ATP synthesis. Protons leak back without passing through ATP synthase, so the chain runs faster and oxygen use rises, while the gradient's energy is released as heat instead of ATP.

lesson_media.alt: Two reaction-coordinate curves share identical reactant and product energies, but the enzyme-catalysed pathway has a lower activation-energy peak.
lesson_media.caption: Enzymes alter kinetics by providing another pathway; they do not supply reaction energy or make an unfavourable equilibrium favourable.

nodes.title: Genomics
nodes.goal: Reading and editing whole genomes.

quiz.prompt: A team designs a CRISPR guide RNA whose 20-base target sequence happens to occur at three separate places in the genome, and delivers it together with Cas9. What should they expect?
quiz.answer: All three sites are cut, not merely the one that was intended
quiz.explain: Cas9 is aimed only by base pairing with its guide and has no way of knowing which match was meant. Every site the guide matches is a substrate, which is why guides are screened for uniqueness and off-target cutting is measured.
choices: Cas9 cuts the matching messenger RNA rather than the DNA
All three sites are cut, not merely the one that was intended
Cas9 compares the three and edits only the real gene
No cutting occurs, because the guide is ambiguous

quiz.prompt: The human genome holds roughly 20,000 protein-coding genes, yet human cells make many more distinct protein species than that. Which explanation fits best?
quiz.answer: One gene can yield several proteins by alternative splicing
quiz.explain: Alternative splicing joins a gene's exons in different combinations, and chemical modification after translation adds further variety. The 20,000 figure is a well-supported count, and non-coding DNA is named for exactly what it does not do.
choices: The gene count is simply an underestimate of the true number
One gene can yield several proteins by alternative splicing
Proteins are copied from other proteins, not from genes
The non-coding DNA between genes codes for the rest

quiz.prompt: A tumour's sequence shows an activating mutation in a kinase for which a targeted inhibitor exists, and the drug works. Six months later the tumour regrows and now carries a second mutation in the same kinase. What is the most likely reading?
quiz.answer: Resistant cells were already present and have now taken over
quiz.explain: A tumour is a genetically varied population under strong selection. Killing the sensitive majority leaves any pre-existing resistant subclone free to expand, which is why resistance mutations so often turn up in the very gene the drug targets.
choices: Resistant cells were already present and have now taken over
A second, unrelated tumour has arisen in the same tissue
The inhibitor itself mutated the gene as a side effect
The first mutation must have been a sequencing error

quiz.prompt: A sequencing run yields 30 million reads of 100 bases each from a genome of 3 billion bases. What is the average fold coverage?
quiz.explain: 30,000,000 x 100 = 3,000,000,000 bases sequenced, which divided by a 3-billion-base genome gives 1x coverage.

quiz.prompt: A genome-wide association study links a common variant to type 2 diabetes with an odds ratio of 1.1. What may be concluded?
quiz.answer: Association is shown, but causation is not shown
choices: The variant must sit inside a gene that causes diabetes
Anyone carrying the variant will develop diabetes
Association is shown, but causation is not shown
Diabetes risk is set by this single gene alone
quiz.explain: An odds ratio of 1.1 is a small shift in population risk, not a prediction about an individual. GWAS hits are usually markers in linkage with the real causal variant and often lie outside any coding sequence.

quiz.prompt: Explain why researchers sequence a patient's tumour and their healthy tissue side by side, rather than the tumour alone.
quiz.answer: Comparing the two lets them subtract the inherited variants present in every cell, so only the somatic mutations that arose in the tumour remain to be studied.
quiz.explain: Everyone carries millions of harmless inherited variants; the matched normal sample is the control that isolates the tumour-specific changes.

quiz.prompt: A GWAS variant carries an odds ratio of 2.0 for a disease. If the baseline odds of disease are 1 in 50, a carrier's odds become 1 in how many?
quiz.explain: Odds of 1 in 50 are 0.02; doubling gives 0.04, which is 1 in 25.

quiz.prompt: A 3.2 gigabase genome is sequenced to 40-fold coverage using 150-base reads. How many million reads are needed? Round to the nearest million.
quiz.explain: Total bases needed are 3.2 billion x 40 = 128 billion. Dividing by 150 gives about 853.3 million reads.

quiz.prompt: A rare variant in a patient's exome is absent from population databases and alters a conserved residue, but the patient's healthy father carries it too. What does this most support?
quiz.answer: The case for this variant alone causing it is weakened
choices: The father's copy must have been miscalled by the sequencer
The case for this variant alone causing it is weakened
The variant is proved harmless by the healthy father
The variant must be causal, since it is so rare
quiz.explain: Rarity and conservation raise suspicion but do not establish causation, and one unaffected carrier does not refute it either: incomplete penetrance, a recessive model or a modifier could each explain him. What the finding removes is the clean segregation the case rested on.

quiz.prompt: Two labs sequence the same tumour sample. One reports a mutation in 3 percent of reads; the other, using ten times fewer reads, does not see it. What is the likeliest reason?
quiz.answer: Shallow coverage easily misses a rare subclone
choices: Sequencing errors invented the variant in the first lab
The second lab used a different reference genome
Shallow coverage easily misses a rare subclone
The mutation arose between the two samplings
quiz.explain: Seeing a variant carried by a few percent of cells needs enough reads over that base to sample it repeatedly. Ten times fewer reads may simply never cover it, and a different reference would not hide a variant that is genuinely there.

lesson_media.alt: A genomics workflow moves from overlapping sequence reads through alignment and variant calling to targeted CRISPR editing and outcome validation.
lesson_media.caption: Genome reading and editing are evidence pipelines; confidence comes from controls, replication, and checking both intended and unintended changes.

nodes.title: Neuroscience
nodes.goal: Neurons, synapses, and the brain.

quiz.prompt: A signal travels along a single neuron as an electrical impulse, but crossing to the next neuron usually requires:
quiz.answer: Chemical neurotransmitters released across a synaptic cleft
quiz.explain: At most synapses the electrical impulse triggers release of neurotransmitters that carry the signal chemically to the next neuron.
choices: Chemical neurotransmitters released across a synaptic cleft
The myelin sheath conducting the signal across the gap
A bridge of shared cytoplasm carrying the charge on
The impulse jumping the gap as a spark of current

quiz.prompt: A drug blocks the receptors that a certain neurotransmitter normally binds to on the receiving neuron. What is the most direct effect?
quiz.answer: The receiving neuron responds less to that transmitter
quiz.explain: Blocking the receptors leaves release and conduction untouched but stops the message being read, so the downstream cell simply responds less. Whether that means more or less firing depends on the transmitter, which the question does not specify.
choices: The presynaptic terminal releases more transmitter at once
The receiving neuron responds less to that transmitter
The receiving neuron fires more, having lost its brake
The sending neuron stops firing action potentials too

quiz.prompt: One patient understands speech normally but cannot produce fluent words. A second speaks fluently, yet the sentences are meaningless and she cannot follow what is said to her. What do the two patients together establish that neither alone would?
quiz.answer: The two abilities depend on separate brain regions
quiz.explain: This is a double dissociation: each ability is lost while the other is spared, in opposite directions. One patient alone is consistent with a single language system damaged by some amount; only the pair rules that out.
choices: The second patient's hearing is what has been damaged
Both patients have one lesion differing only in size
The two abilities depend on separate brain regions
Language must be confined to the left hemisphere

quiz.prompt: An axon conducts an impulse at 50 metres per second. How many milliseconds does the signal take to travel 1 metre?
quiz.explain: Time = 1 / 50 second = 0.02 s, which is 20 milliseconds.

quiz.prompt: In multiple sclerosis the myelin sheath around central axons is progressively destroyed. What change in conduction would you predict?
quiz.answer: Conduction slows or fails in the stretches between nodes
choices: The axon can no longer generate any action potentials at all
Conduction slows or fails in the stretches between nodes
Only the cell body is affected, so conduction is normal
Impulses travel faster with less material in the way
quiz.explain: Myelin lets the impulse jump from node to node and stops charge leaking away in between. Strip it and the axon must conduct continuously through a leaky membrane, so the signal is slowed or blocked even though the axon can still fire.

quiz.prompt: A toxin prevents synaptic vesicles from fusing with the presynaptic membrane at the neuromuscular junction. What is the predicted result?
quiz.answer: Flaccid paralysis, since no transmitter is released at all
choices: Flaccid paralysis, since no transmitter is released at all
Acetylcholine builds up in the cleft and overstimulates
The motor neuron can no longer fire action potentials
The muscle contracts continuously and fails to relax
quiz.explain: The action potential still reaches the terminal, but without vesicle fusion no acetylcholine crosses the cleft, so the muscle is never depolarised. Continuous contraction is what happens when transmitter is not cleared, the opposite fault.

quiz.prompt: A neuron rests at -70 mV and fires when it reaches a threshold of -55 mV. How many millivolts of depolarisation are needed to reach threshold?
quiz.explain: From -70 mV to -55 mV is a 15 mV depolarisation.

quiz.prompt: A myelinated axon conducts at 80 metres per second; an unmyelinated one conducts at 0.5 metres per second. How many times faster is the myelinated axon?
quiz.explain: 80 divided by 0.5 is 160.

quiz.prompt: A drug blocks the transporter that recovers a neurotransmitter from the synaptic cleft, but does not touch the receptors. What is the most direct consequence?
quiz.answer: The transmitter lingers in the cleft and acts for longer
choices: The presynaptic terminal runs out of transmitter at once
The transmitter lingers in the cleft and acts for longer
The postsynaptic cell stops responding immediately
Less transmitter is released with each impulse
quiz.explain: Reuptake is the main way the signal is switched off. Block the transporter and the same quantity of transmitter released stays in the cleft, so it keeps binding receptors and the effect is prolonged rather than reduced.

quiz.prompt: Immediately after an action potential, even a very strong stimulus fails to trigger a second one. Which explanation fits?
quiz.answer: Sodium channels are still inactivated and cannot reopen
choices: The membrane is hyperpolarised below its resting level
Sodium channels are still inactivated and cannot reopen
The membrane is already sitting above threshold
The axon has run out of neurotransmitter
quiz.explain: Inactivated sodium channels cannot reopen however large the stimulus until the membrane has repolarised and reset them. That absolute block, not the membrane voltage alone, is what caps firing rate and keeps the impulse travelling one way.

lesson_media.alt: A membrane-potential graph labels resting potential near minus 70 millivolts, threshold near minus 55, sodium-driven depolarisation, potassium-driven repolarisation, and the undershoot back to rest.
lesson_media.caption: The phase labels connect voltage changes to channel events and separate threshold crossing from the later calcium-triggered chemical signal at the synapse.

nodes.title: Evolutionary Biology
nodes.goal: Population genetics and phylogenetics.

quiz.prompt: In a large population at Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, a recessive allele has frequency q = 0.2. What is the frequency p of the dominant allele?
quiz.explain: Because the two allele frequencies must sum to 1, p = 1 minus 0.2, which equals 0.8.

quiz.prompt: In a large population at Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, a recessive allele has frequency q = 0.2. What fraction of individuals are expected to be homozygous recessive (frequency q squared)?
quiz.explain: The homozygous recessive frequency is q squared, and 0.2 squared equals 0.04.

quiz.prompt: On a phylogenetic tree, two species share a more recent common ancestor with each other than either does with a third species. What does this indicate?
quiz.answer: The two are the more closely related pair of the three
quiz.explain: Relatedness on a tree is a matter of how recently lineages shared an ancestor, not how alike they look. Living species are one another's cousins, never one another's ancestors, and none is further along any ladder.
choices: The third species is the direct ancestor of the other two
The two are the more closely related pair of the three
The two must resemble each other more than the third
The third species is the least evolved of the three

quiz.prompt: Convergent evolution is the independent appearance of similar form in unrelated lineages under similar selection. A researcher wants to establish that the streamlined, finned body of ichthyosaurs, sharks and dolphins is convergent rather than inherited from a shared ancestor. Which evidence would decide it?
quiz.answer: Their closest relatives lack the streamlined shape
choices: The three groups share many other features besides shape
The shape appears in the fossil record at the same date
Their closest relatives lack the streamlined shape
All three are fast swimmers in open water
quiz.explain: The question is settled by where the trait sits on the tree, not by how alike the animals look. If each lineage's nearest relatives lack the shape, it must have arisen separately three times; a trait inherited from a common ancestor would show up in those relatives too.

quiz.prompt: Genetic drift changes allele frequencies through the chance sampling of who survives and breeds; natural selection changes them because the allele itself affects survival. A storm kills 90 percent of a beetle population and the survivors' allele frequencies differ from before. Which further observation would point to drift rather than selection?
quiz.answer: A nearby population was shifted the opposite way by it
choices: The surviving beetles are darker than the population mean was
A nearby population was shifted the opposite way by it
The shift persisted into the following generation
The storm removed nine beetles out of every ten
quiz.explain: Selection pushes independent populations in the same direction, because the same trait pays in both. Chance pushes them wherever the sampling happens to fall, so opposite shifts under the same storm are the signature of sampling rather than of the allele mattering.

quiz.prompt: Two bird populations separated by a new reservoir stop interbreeding, and after many generations their hybrids are infertile. Name the process and explain how it worked.
quiz.answer: This is allopatric speciation: a geographic barrier stopped gene flow, the separated populations diverged through drift and different selection, and reproductive isolation built up as a by-product.
quiz.explain: Geographic separation is the commonest route to new species: isolation removes gene flow, and independent evolutionary change then makes the populations incompatible.

quiz.prompt: In a Hardy-Weinberg population, 9 percent of individuals are homozygous recessive. Give the expected frequency of heterozygotes as a decimal.
quiz.explain: q squared is 0.09, so q = 0.3 and p = 0.7. Heterozygotes are 2pq = 2 x 0.7 x 0.3 = 0.42.

quiz.prompt: A selectively neutral allele sits at frequency 0.4 in a very large population with no selection, no migration and no mutation. What is its expected frequency after 10 generations?
quiz.explain: Hardy-Weinberg conditions leave allele frequencies unchanged from generation to generation; only the genotype proportions settle.

quiz.prompt: A trait's frequency swings sharply between generations on a small island but stays steady in a large mainland population, with selection identical in both. What accounts for the contrast?
quiz.answer: Chance sampling has more effect when numbers are small
choices: Island generations turn over far faster than mainland ones
Chance sampling has more effect when numbers are small
The island population is under much stronger selection
Migrants keep bringing new alleles to the island
quiz.explain: Drift is sampling error in who happens to reproduce, and the error in a sample shrinks as the sample grows. With selection held equal in the two places, the small population is the one whose frequencies wander.

quiz.prompt: Two lizard forms meet in a narrow contact zone, hybridise there, and the hybrids leave few offspring. Over generations, what does selection favour in the parental forms near that zone?
quiz.answer: Choosier mating within each of the two forms
choices: Loss of the traits that tell the two forms apart
Choosier mating within each of the two forms
Hybrids that survive better, widening the zone
Greater movement of adults into the zone
quiz.explain: Hybridising wastes reproductive effort when the hybrids leave few offspring, so individuals that avoid it leave more descendants. Selection therefore strengthens the cues and preferences that keep the forms apart, which is reinforcement.

lesson_media.alt: A population-genetics network separates non-random selection from random genetic drift and connects inherited divergence to phylogenetic inference.
lesson_media.caption: Evolutionary biology explains frequency change with multiple mechanisms and tests lineage relationships using shared derived evidence.

nodes.title: Systems Physiology
nodes.goal: Homeostasis and control across the body.

quiz.prompt: Insulin release after a meal is negative feedback: the rise in blood glucose triggers the very response that lowers it. In a person whose insulin-releasing cells have been destroyed, what happens to blood glucose after a meal?
quiz.answer: It rises after the meal and stays high far longer
quiz.explain: Negative feedback works by opposing a disturbance. Removing the effector takes away the correcting arm but not the disturbance, so glucose still climbs after the meal and is simply never brought back down.
choices: It stays flat, because the loop is broken both ways
It rises after the meal and stays high far longer
It falls below normal, since nothing raises it
It swings up and down faster than before

quiz.prompt: On a cold day your body shivers and the blood vessels in your skin narrow. What is the combined physiological purpose of these responses?
quiz.answer: To generate heat and to reduce loss from the skin
quiz.explain: Shivering turns muscle work into heat, and narrowing the skin vessels keeps warm blood in the core where it cannot be lost. Sending blood to the skin is what the body does to shed heat, not to conserve it.
choices: To move warm blood out to the skin where the cold is
To generate heat and to reduce loss from the skin
To slow the heart so less warm blood is lost
To cool the body quickly, as sweating does

quiz.prompt: Two signals leave the brain at the same instant: a nerve impulse to one muscle, and a hormone released into the bloodstream. Which description of their arrival and duration is right?
quiz.answer: The nerve signal arrives first; the hormone lasts longer
quiz.explain: Nervous signalling is fast and brief: an electrical impulse delivered straight to a named target and switched off in milliseconds. Endocrine signalling is slower to arrive, since the hormone must travel in the blood, but lasts as long as the hormone keeps circulating.
choices: Both arrive together, but the nerve effect lasts longer
The nerve signal arrives first; the hormone lasts longer
Both arrive together and both fade at the same rate
Hormone first, and its effect also fades first

quiz.prompt: A person breathes 12 times a minute with a tidal volume of 500 mL. What is their minute ventilation in millilitres per minute?
quiz.explain: Minute ventilation is tidal volume times breathing rate: 500 x 12 = 6000 mL per minute.

quiz.prompt: After a long run with nothing to drink, blood plasma becomes more concentrated. Which response restores the balance?
quiz.answer: ADH release makes the kidney's ducts reabsorb far more water
choices: ADH release makes the kidney's ducts reabsorb far more water
The kidney produces more dilute urine to flush out salt
Aldosterone rises so the kidney holds on to more sodium
The gut absorbs extra salt from the food that was eaten
quiz.explain: Osmoreceptors sense the rise in plasma osmolarity and trigger ADH, which makes the collecting duct permeable so water is conserved and the urine concentrated. The problem is a shortage of water, not an excess of sodium, so holding sodium would make it worse.

quiz.prompt: During a severe asthma attack a patient's arterial pH falls to 7.25 and their carbon dioxide level is high. What is the most likely cause?
quiz.answer: Retained carbon dioxide forming carbonic acid
choices: The muscles of breathing produce extra lactic acid
Loss of stomach acid through repeated vomiting
Retained carbon dioxide forming carbonic acid
Excess bicarbonate released by the kidneys
quiz.explain: The clue is that carbon dioxide is high as well as pH low. Poor ventilation traps carbon dioxide, which reacts with water to give carbonic acid: respiratory acidosis. A metabolic acid load would drive carbon dioxide down, not up.

quiz.prompt: During exercise a person's stroke volume is 80 mL and heart rate 150 beats per minute. Give the cardiac output in litres per minute.
quiz.explain: 80 mL x 150 = 12,000 mL per minute, which is 12 litres per minute.

quiz.prompt: Glomerular filtration rate is 125 mL per minute and 99 percent of the filtrate is reabsorbed. How many millilitres of urine are formed per minute?
quiz.explain: One percent of 125 mL is 1.25 mL per minute.

quiz.prompt: An anxious patient hyperventilates and their arterial pH climbs to 7.50. Which mechanism explains the shift?
quiz.answer: Losing carbon dioxide leaves less carbonic acid
choices: The extra oxygen breathed in makes the blood alkaline
The kidneys have already retained extra bicarbonate
Losing carbon dioxide leaves less carbonic acid
Stress hormones raise the blood pH directly
quiz.explain: Carbon dioxide and water form carbonic acid, so blowing carbon dioxide off faster than it is made pulls that equilibrium back and raises pH: respiratory alkalosis. Renal handling of bicarbonate takes days, far too slow to explain a change in minutes.

quiz.prompt: A person drinks two litres of water in a few minutes. What would you predict over the following hour?
quiz.answer: ADH falls and dilute urine is passed
choices: Aldosterone climbs sharply to hold on to sodium
ADH secretion rises to clear the extra water
ADH falls and dilute urine is passed
The thirst centre is stimulated more
quiz.explain: The load dilutes the plasma, and falling osmolarity switches ADH release off. Without ADH the collecting ducts stay impermeable to water, so the excess leaves as a large volume of dilute urine.

lesson_media.alt: A negative-feedback loop shows rising body temperature detected by sensors, compared by the hypothalamus, and reduced by sweating and skin blood flow.
lesson_media.caption: Homeostasis is active regulation: effectors change heat transfer in the direction that reduces deviation from the controlled range.

nodes.title: Animal Behaviour
nodes.goal: Why animals do what they do: instinct, learning, and the logic of the wild.

quiz.prompt: A newly hatched gosling follows the first moving object it sees during a brief critical window, even if that object is a human researcher rather than its mother. Name this phenomenon and classify it as innate or learned.
quiz.answer: Imprinting — a form of rapid, time-limited learning
quiz.explain: Konrad Lorenz's classic studies named this filial imprinting. It is learned, not hardwired to a specific stimulus, but the WINDOW in which it can be learned, and the drive to attach to whatever qualifies, are innate — a striking case where learning and instinct are not opposites but work together.
choices: Imprinting — a form of rapid, time-limited learning
A fixed action pattern, entirely innate with no learning involved
Classical conditioning, requiring dozens of paired trials
Habituation to a repeated harmless stimulus

quiz.prompt: Kin selection theory (Hamilton's rule) predicts a costly helping behaviour will be favoured by evolution when rB > C, where r is genetic relatedness, B the benefit to the recipient, and C the cost to the helper. A ground squirrel gives an alarm call that draws a predator's attention to itself, warning nearby squirrels. Which relationship makes this most likely to evolve?
quiz.answer: The nearby squirrels are close kin, raising r and the rB term
quiz.explain: Alarm calling is a textbook costly-helping behaviour, and field studies of Belding's ground squirrels found callers were more likely to have close relatives nearby. A gene that costs its bearer but saves several close relatives (high r) can still spread, because those relatives carry copies of the same gene — the gene is helping copies of itself, not the individual as such.
choices: The nearby squirrels are close kin, raising r and the rB term
The predator is rare, so C is effectively zero regardless of relatedness
The caller is old and near the end of its reproductive life
The group is large, which lowers r for every individual

quiz.prompt: Explain the difference between a fixed action pattern and a learned behaviour, using the example of a male stickleback fish attacking a crude red-bellied model even though it looks nothing like a real rival fish.
quiz.answer: A fixed action pattern is a stereotyped, largely innate sequence of behaviour triggered by a simple, specific cue called a sign stimulus or releaser — here, a patch of red on the underside. The behaviour fires reliably in response to that one cue, exaggerated versions of the cue provoke it even more strongly (a supernormal stimulus), and the animal does not need prior experience to perform it. This contrasts with learned behaviour, which is acquired through individual experience and can be modified by it; the stickleback's attack response is present from the first time a male encounters the trigger, without any learning trial.
quiz.explain: Niko Tinbergen's stickleback experiments were foundational in showing that complex-looking behaviour can be driven by a narrow, simple trigger rather than by recognising the whole animal.

quiz.prompt: A wolf pack cooperatively hunts prey too large for any single wolf to bring down alone. A biologist proposes explaining this purely via kin selection, since packs are usually family groups. A colleague objects that reciprocal altruism could also explain cooperative hunting even among unrelated wolves. Evaluate whether these two explanations are mutually exclusive.
quiz.answer: No — both mechanisms can operate simultaneously and are not mutually exclusive
quiz.explain: Kin selection (favoring relatives who share your genes) and reciprocal altruism (trading favours over repeated interactions, even among non-relatives, provided cheaters are punished or excluded) are distinct mechanisms that can both push toward the same behaviour. Real cooperative hunting in wolves likely reflects both: packs are often kin groups, AND each hunt's benefits are shared in ways that make defection costly even to an unrelated member. Evolutionary explanations for a single behaviour are not required to pick exactly one mechanism.
choices: No — both mechanisms can operate simultaneously and are not mutually exclusive
Yes — kin selection can only explain behaviour in genetically related groups
Yes — reciprocal altruism requires unrelated individuals by definition, ruling out overlap
Neither mechanism can explain cooperative hunting; it must be pure group selection

quiz.prompt: A rat is repeatedly given a mild electric shock a few seconds after a tone plays, and it soon begins to freeze at the sound of the tone alone, before any shock. Identify the type of learning and its key components.
quiz.answer: Classical conditioning — tone (CS) predicts shock (US), producing freezing (CR)
quiz.explain: This is Pavlovian/classical conditioning: an initially neutral stimulus (the tone, becoming a conditioned stimulus, CS) is paired with a stimulus that already triggers a response (the shock, an unconditioned stimulus, US, provoking an unconditioned response). After pairing, the CS alone provokes a learned response (freezing, now a conditioned response, CR). This differs from operant conditioning, where the animal's own behaviour, not a paired stimulus, is what gets reinforced or punished.
choices: Classical conditioning — tone (CS) predicts shock (US), producing freezing (CR)
Operant conditioning — freezing is reinforced by shock avoidance
Habituation — the rat is simply getting used to the tone
Latent learning — the rat is exploring without any reinforcement present

quiz.prompt: Vervet monkeys use acoustically distinct alarm calls for different predators — one call for leopards (prompting a scramble into trees), a different call for eagles (prompting a duck into bushes), and a third for snakes (prompting a scan of the ground). A skeptic argues these are just generic "I'm scared" signals rather than functionally referential communication. What observation would best refute the skeptic?
quiz.answer: Playing back a recorded call alone (no predator present) triggers the predator-specific response
quiz.explain: This is exactly the experiment Seyfarth, Cheney, and Marler ran: playing a leopard call through a hidden speaker, with no leopard anywhere near, still sent the monkeys scrambling into trees, and the eagle call still sent them into bushes. Because the response tracked the CALL itself rather than any actual predator or general arousal, it demonstrated the calls function referentially — they encode which threat is present, not just that something is threatening.
choices: Playing back a recorded call alone (no predator present) triggers the predator-specific response
Observing that monkeys call more loudly when more predators are nearby
Noting that infant monkeys give alarm calls less often than adults
Showing that calls happen more often during the day than at night

quiz.prompt: Under Hamilton's rule rB > C, a helper shares relatedness r = 0.25 with a half-sibling's offspring (a niece or nephew) and the cost of helping is 4 units of the helper's own fitness. What is the minimum benefit B to the recipient needed for the helping gene to be favoured by selection?
quiz.explain: Hamilton's rule requires rB > C, so B > C/r = 4/0.25 = 16. The smallest whole-number benefit strictly exceeding 16 is 17.

quiz.prompt: Tinbergen proposed four complementary questions for any behaviour: mechanism (how does it work physiologically), ontogeny (how does it develop in the individual), survival value/function (what is it for), and phylogeny (how did it evolve historically). A student studying birdsong learning asks only "which brain regions control song production?" Which of Tinbergen's four questions does this address, and which are left untouched?
quiz.answer: Mechanism only; ontogeny, function, and phylogeny remain unanswered
quiz.explain: Tinbergen's four questions are proximate (mechanism, ontogeny) and ultimate (function, phylogeny) causes, and they are complementary, not competing — a full account of any behaviour needs all four. Asking only about brain circuitry answers the mechanistic question but says nothing about how the behaviour develops through experience, why it evolved, or its evolutionary history across species.
choices: Mechanism only; ontogeny, function, and phylogeny remain unanswered
Function only, since brain regions evolved for a survival purpose
All four questions at once, since mechanism underlies the other three
Phylogeny only, since brain structure reflects evolutionary history

quiz.prompt: Explain why altruistic behaviour toward non-kin, such as vampire bats regurgitating blood to feed hungry unrelated roost-mates who fed them on a previous night, is not a straightforward contradiction of "selfish gene" evolutionary theory.
quiz.answer: This is reciprocal altruism: a bat that shares blood today is more likely to receive shared blood on a future night it goes hungry itself, so the behaviour pays off over repeated interactions even without any genetic relatedness. Bats appear to track who has and hasn't reciprocated, and preferentially share with past reciprocators, which keeps the system stable against cheaters (individuals who take help but never give it) by letting bats withhold future help from non-reciprocators. So the gene for reciprocating is still ultimately self-interested at the level of long-run expected fitness, even though any single act looks selfless.
quiz.explain: Robert Trivers' reciprocal altruism theory, later supported by Gerald Wilkinson's field studies of vampire bats, showed that apparent selflessness toward non-kin can still be evolutionarily stable once repeated interaction and cheater-detection are in place.

quiz.prompt: Optimal foraging theory predicts an animal should abandon a depleting food patch once its intake rate there drops below the average intake rate available across the whole habitat (the marginal value theorem). A bird stays in a berry patch well past that point even as nearby patches sit richer and untouched. Propose the most likely explanation consistent with the theory rather than against it.
quiz.answer: Travel cost to the next patch is high enough to raise the patch's true giving-up threshold
quiz.explain: The marginal value theorem already builds in travel time/cost between patches — the optimal giving-up time rises as travel cost rises, since abandoning a patch is only worthwhile if the trip pays for itself. A bird facing a long or risky flight to the next patch can rationally linger in a depleting patch longer than a naive glance at instantaneous intake rates would suggest, without the theory being wrong.
choices: Travel cost to the next patch is high enough to raise the patch's true giving-up threshold
The bird is simply behaving irrationally and the theory has been falsified
Optimal foraging theory only applies to solitary, not social, foragers
The richer patches must be an illusion, since animals never leave value on the table

lesson_media.alt: A behaviour table contrasts inherited responses, learned responses, and cooperation by source, fitness trade-off, and experimental test.
lesson_media.caption: Ethology asks both proximate questions about mechanisms and ultimate questions about evolutionary consequences; either alone is incomplete.

nodes.title: Systems & Synthetic Biology
nodes.goal: Networks of genes; engineering living cells.

quiz.prompt: A human gene is put into E. coli under a bacterial promoter. The gene is transcribed, but no protein appears. When the same gene's cDNA is used instead, the protein is made. What does that show?
quiz.answer: Bacteria cannot splice the introns out of the transcript
quiz.explain: The genetic code is essentially universal, so bacterial ribosomes read a human message perfectly well. What bacteria lack is a spliceosome, so a genomic gene is transcribed with its introns still in; cDNA, copied from mature mRNA, has none.
choices: The genetic code differs between the two species
Bacteria cannot splice the introns out of the transcript
Bacterial ribosomes cannot read human codons
The human protein is toxic to the bacterial cell

quiz.prompt: Knocking out each of three genes on its own changes nothing measurable, but knocking out all three together collapses the phenotype. What does that pattern argue for?
quiz.answer: The three genes back one another up
quiz.explain: Parallel, partly redundant routes give exactly this signature: while any one route survives, the output is buffered. Genes arranged in a single chain would fail the moment one link was cut, and no single gene can account for two silent knockouts.
choices: The three genes act in one linear chain, each needed in turn
The three genes back one another up
Only the last gene knocked out does the real work
The single knockouts must have been incomplete

quiz.prompt: A synthetic biosensor wires a toxin-sensing promoter to a gene for a glowing protein. In testing, the cells glow faintly even when no toxin is present. Which change would most improve the sensor?
quiz.answer: Tighten the promoter so that it leaks less when off
quiz.explain: Glow with no toxin is leak from the promoter's off state, and every change that scales the whole output - a brighter reporter, more copies, longer incubation - scales that background with it. Only cutting the off-state output improves the ratio the sensor depends on.
choices: Swap in a brighter reporter protein to raise the signal
Tighten the promoter so that it leaks less when off
Read the glow after a much longer incubation
Add many more copies of the sensor construct

quiz.prompt: A synthetic repressilator oscillates with a period of 150 minutes. How many complete oscillations occur over 10 hours?
quiz.explain: 10 hours is 600 minutes, and 600 divided by 150 gives 4 complete cycles.

quiz.prompt: A transcription factor represses its own promoter. Modelling and measurement both show what this negative autoregulation does, compared with an unregulated gene at the same steady-state level:
quiz.answer: It settles at its set point faster and fluctuates less
choices: It rises more slowly and swings more widely in level
It settles at its set point faster and fluctuates less
It creates a sharp switch with two stable states
It makes the response slower but far more precise
quiz.explain: Negative autoregulation is the commonest network motif in E. coli for two reasons at once: a strong promoter drives the level up quickly, then repression catches it at the set point, and any excursion above or below is pushed back.

quiz.prompt: A toggle switch built from two mutually repressing genes is bistable: it settles into one of two states and stays there. A brief pulse of an inducer that inactivates repressor A is applied and then washed out. What do you predict?
quiz.answer: The circuit flips to the other state and stays there
choices: Both repressors end up expressed at equal middling levels
The circuit flips to the other state and stays there
It returns to its original state once the pulse ends
It oscillates between the two states from then on
quiz.explain: Bistability means each state maintains itself, so a transient push that carries the system past the unstable midpoint leaves it in the new state after the push is gone. That memory is what makes the toggle a switch rather than a sensor.

quiz.prompt: A synthetic genetic oscillator in a bacterium has a period of 90 minutes. How many complete cycles occur over 9 hours?
quiz.explain: Nine hours is 540 minutes, and 540 divided by 90 is 6 cycles.

quiz.prompt: A promoter makes a protein at 120 molecules per cell per minute, and the protein is removed with a half-life of 30 minutes. Steady state is production divided by the rate constant k = 0.693/30 per minute. Give the steady-state number of molecules to the nearest hundred.
quiz.explain: k = 0.693/30 = 0.0231 per minute, so the steady-state level is 120/0.0231 = about 5,195 molecules, or 5,200 to the nearest hundred.

quiz.prompt: A well-characterised genetic circuit is moved intact from E. coli into yeast and barely functions, though every part is present. Which explanation should be checked first?
quiz.answer: The host reads the very same parts differently
choices: Yeast lacks the ribosomes needed for these proteins
The host reads the very same parts differently
The circuit's DNA must have mutated during transfer
Yeast reads a different genetic code from bacteria
quiz.explain: Parts are not context-free. Bacterial promoters, ribosome binding sites and codon preferences are handled differently by eukaryotic polymerase and ribosomes, so the circuit has to be rebuilt for the new chassis. The genetic code is the one thing that does carry over.

quiz.prompt: A metabolic engineer doubles the amount of the first enzyme in a pathway and product yield rises by only 3 percent. What does this most directly indicate?
quiz.answer: Control of the flux lies elsewhere
choices: The extra enzyme is broken down as fast as it is made
The product is used up as made
The enzyme was probably not overexpressed at all
Control of the flux lies elsewhere
quiz.explain: Flux control is distributed across a pathway, and the first step often carries very little of it. A flux control coefficient near zero means the rate is set somewhere else - a later enzyme, a cofactor, a precursor - so more of this one enzyme buys almost nothing.

lesson_media.alt: A synthetic gene circuit converts an input signal through sensor, regulator, and output genes, then feeds measured product back to repress the sensor.
lesson_media.caption: Systems biology explains phenotype from interactions and dynamics; synthetic biology tests that understanding by constructing controlled circuits.

nodes.title: Developmental Biology
nodes.goal: From one cell to a whole organism.

lesson_media.alt: One signal source faces a row of eleven cells; a fading concentration wash crosses two threshold markers and divides the cells into three colored fate regions.
lesson_media.caption: In this threshold model, one source makes a decaying morphogen gradient. Otherwise-equivalent cells read their local concentration against two thresholds to produce three spatial fates.

lesson_media.title: Read a morphogen gradient
lesson_media.instructions: Inspect the concentration and fate at each of eleven cells. Flatten the signal to one intermediate concentration, then restore the gradient and compare the three explicit fate regions.

quiz.prompt: A typical nucleated somatic cell switches on muscle proteins and differentiates into a muscle fibre. Which statement best describes what usually happened to its genetic information?
quiz.answer: It retained essentially the same genome but changed which genes it expresses
quiz.explain: Differentiation mainly changes gene regulation and expression rather than replacing the genome with a cell-type-specific version. 'Essentially' matters: somatic mutations and specialized DNA rearrangements can occur, and a few mature cell types lose their nucleus, so literal genomic identity is not a universal rule.
choices: Its DNA has been rewritten into a muscle-specific version
It retained essentially the same genome but changed which genes it expresses
It has gained muscle genes it did not previously have
It has discarded the genes it will never use again
