quiz.prompt: A lab needs one starting cell line from which it can grow heart muscle, neurons and liver tissue for drug testing. Why do embryonic stem cells suit that job?
quiz.answer: They can give rise to nearly any cell type in the body
quiz.explain: Pluripotency, not speed of division, is what the job needs: a single line that can be pushed down the heart, neural and liver routes. A cell already committed to one fate, or to a narrow set of fates, could not supply all three.
choices: They can give rise to nearly any cell type in the body
They are already specialised and locked into one fate
They can become skin or blood cells but nothing else
They divide faster than any specialised cell does

quiz.prompt: During development, a chemical signal (a morphogen) is released from one end of an embryo, forming a concentration gradient. How can this single signal help create different structures along the embryo?
quiz.answer: Different concentrations can activate different programs and bias or specify different fates
quiz.explain: A morphogen gradient can carry positional information: cells exposed to different local concentrations may activate different gene-regulatory programs and adopt different fates. Simple threshold diagrams are useful idealizations; response also depends on exposure time, cellular competence and other signals.
choices: Every cell receives the same dose and reacts identically
Different concentrations can activate different programs and bias or specify different fates
The signal reaches only the cells nearest its source
The gradient decides the timing rather than the fate

quiz.prompt: Tissue from the dorsal lip of an amphibian gastrula is grafted onto the belly of a second embryo, and a second body axis forms largely out of host cells. What does this experiment show about the grafted tissue?
quiz.answer: The dorsal lip acts as an organizer: it releases signals that induce neighbouring host cells to change their fate and pattern an entire new axis.
quiz.explain: Because the extra axis is built mainly from host tissue, the graft cannot simply have become the new axis itself; it must have instructed its neighbours. This is the Spemann-Mangold organizer.

quiz.prompt: A fly mutant grows a pair of legs in the sockets where its antennae belong. Which class of gene has most likely been mis-expressed?
quiz.answer: A Hox gene that specifies segment identity
choices: A gene controlling how many segments the fly forms
A gene coding for a structural protein of the leg
A gene needed to supply the antenna with nutrients
A Hox gene that specifies segment identity
quiz.explain: A complete, well-formed leg in the wrong socket means the machinery for building legs is intact and has simply been switched on in the wrong place. That points to a selector gene of identity, not to a builder of structure or a counter of segments.

quiz.prompt: Adult fibroblasts forced to express four transcription factors can be reprogrammed to a pluripotent state and then form many tissues. What does this most directly show about differentiation?
quiz.answer: Its regulatory state can be reversed because most genomic information was retained
choices: Differentiated cells must discard genes as they specialise
Its regulatory state can be reversed because most genomic information was retained
Pluripotency exists only in cells taken from an embryo
The four factors must add new genes to the genome
quiz.explain: Induced pluripotency shows that a differentiated regulatory state can be reset and that the cells retained the genomic information needed for many other fates. It does not require every DNA base to be literally unchanged: somatic mutations or rearrangements may remain, and reprogramming is neither perfect nor universal.

quiz.prompt: A sea urchin zygote goes through 7 rounds of synchronous cleavage with no cell loss. How many cells result?
quiz.explain: Each round doubles the count, so 2 to the power 7 is 128 cells.

quiz.prompt: In an idealized threshold model, this morphogen is the only positional cue, all cells respond identically, and their thresholds stay fixed. The gradient is flattened so every cell sees the same intermediate concentration. What outcome does the model predict?
quiz.answer: One intermediate fate everywhere, and no pattern at all
choices: Development proceeds normally, since the signal is still there
One intermediate fate everywhere, and no pattern at all
Cells take random fates in a salt-and-pepper arrangement
Only the highest-threshold fate is produced
quiz.explain: Under the stated assumptions, every cell applies the same fixed thresholds to the same concentration, so every cell adopts the same intermediate fate and the spatial pattern disappears. Real embryos also use timing, competence and interacting signals, which is why the assumptions are explicit.

quiz.prompt: Posterior tissue from one limb bud is grafted to the anterior edge of a second bud, and a mirror-image duplicated limb develops. Lineage tracing shows that most extra digits are made from host cells rather than graft cells. Which interpretation fits best?
quiz.answer: The tissue is a source of positional signal
choices: The graft simply supplied extra cells that became the new digits
Limb identity was already fixed before the bud formed
The graft physically split the bud into two halves
The tissue is a source of positional signal
quiz.explain: A mirror-image duplication is the signature of a second source of the same graded signal, read from the opposite side. That host cells, not graft cells, build most of the extra digits is what rules out the graft merely supplying the material.

quiz.prompt: A drug given to a pregnant animal causes severe limb defects only during a narrow window of a few days, and has no effect if given earlier or later. Explain what this reveals about development.
quiz.answer: Development runs through critical periods. The limb is being specified and patterned during that window, so disrupting it then leaves a permanent defect, while the same drug before or after meets tissues that are not yet sensitive, or have already committed and moved on.
quiz.explain: Teratogen sensitivity is stage-dependent rather than dose-dependent alone, which is why the timing of an exposure matters as much as its size.

nodes.title: Immunology
nodes.goal: The immune system in depth.

quiz.prompt: A serum raised against one influenza strain neutralises that strain completely but does nothing against a closely related one. The two strains differ at only a few surface residues. What does this show?
quiz.answer: Binding depends on the exact shape of a small surface patch
quiz.explain: An antibody's binding site is complementary to one epitope, a patch of a few residues. Change those residues and the fit is lost, which is why recognition is of a particular surface and not of the organism as a whole.
choices: Binding depends on the exact shape of a small surface patch
Antibodies recognise a pathogen as a whole organism
One antibody binds anything it meets equally well
The serum has simply lost potency between the tests

quiz.prompt: A virus hides and replicates inside the body's own cells. Which immune response is most important for destroying those already-infected cells?
quiz.answer: Cytotoxic T cells that kill infected cells
quiz.explain: Antibodies mainly target free pathogens, while cytotoxic T cells recognize and destroy the body's own infected cells.
choices: Circulating antibodies that neutralize free virus particles
Phagocytes that engulf virus particles in the bloodstream
Cytotoxic T cells that kill infected cells
Mucus and cilia lining the surface of the airway

quiz.prompt: Self-tolerance is the deletion or suppression of lymphocytes that react strongly to the body's own molecules, and it is imposed mainly as lymphocytes develop. In type 1 diabetes, T cells destroy the person's own insulin-producing cells. Which conclusion follows from that definition?
quiz.answer: Some self-reactive clones escaped the developmental screen
quiz.explain: If tolerance is a screen applied during development, autoimmunity is a failure of that screen: clones that should have been removed survived and have found their target. The target cells are unaltered; what changed is which lymphocytes were let through.
choices: Some self-reactive clones escaped the developmental screen
Tolerance was lost across every lymphocyte at once
Insulin itself must have been altered by the disease
The patient's lymphocytes never developed at all

quiz.prompt: During a secondary response an antibody titre doubles each day. Starting at 200 units, what is the titre after 5 days?
quiz.explain: Five doublings multiply the titre by 32: 200 x 32 = 6400 units.

quiz.prompt: Cytotoxic T cells kill a cell that displays a foreign peptide on MHC class I. Natural killer cells apply the opposite rule and kill a cell that displays no MHC class I at all. A virus makes infected cells strip MHC class I from their surface. What follows for the virus?
quiz.answer: It hides from cytotoxic T cells but not from NK cells
choices: It hides from cytotoxic T cells but not from NK cells
It becomes visible to T cells and hidden from NK cells
Neither is affected, as MHC matters only in transplants
It hides from both, since neither can now see the cell
quiz.explain: Removing MHC class I takes away the display T cells inspect, but the absence of that display is itself the signal NK cells act on. The two rules are complementary, so escaping one opens the door to the other.

quiz.prompt: A traveller given a shot of donor antibodies is protected for a few weeks, while a vaccinated traveller is protected for years. Explain the difference.
quiz.answer: The donor antibodies give passive immunity: they are gradually broken down and no memory is made. Vaccination gives active immunity, in which the person's own B and T memory cells persist and respond fast on later exposure.
quiz.explain: Passive transfer is immediate but temporary; active immunisation is slower to establish but leaves a memory compartment that can be recalled for years.

quiz.prompt: An antibody binds its antigen with a dissociation constant Kd of 2 nM. At what free antigen concentration, in nanomolar, is half of the antibody occupied?
quiz.explain: Kd is by definition the ligand concentration at which half the binding sites are occupied, so 2 nM.

quiz.prompt: In a vaccine trial there are 5 cases among 10,000 vaccinated people and 100 cases among 10,000 controls. Give the vaccine efficacy as a percentage.
quiz.explain: Efficacy is (100 - 5) / 100 = 0.95, or 95 percent reduction in the attack rate.

quiz.prompt: A patient with no B cells but normal T cells has repeated severe bacterial infections in the blood and lungs, yet clears most viral infections adequately. Which conclusion is best supported?
quiz.answer: Antibody matters most against organisms outside cells
choices: Antibody matters most against organisms outside cells
B cells matter only for long-term immune memory
T cells cannot respond at all without B cells
Antibody's main job is to activate T cells
quiz.explain: Antibody opsonises and neutralises pathogens in blood and on surfaces, which is why losing B cells leaves someone open to extracellular bacteria. Viruses inside cells are dealt with largely by T cells, which this patient still has.

quiz.prompt: A transplanted kidney turns dark and fails within minutes of the surgeon restoring blood flow, far too fast for any new T cell response. Which mechanism best fits?
quiz.answer: Antibodies already present attacked the graft vessels
choices: Antibodies already present attacked the graft vessels
Cytotoxic T cells killed the graft cells immediately
The graft's own immune cells attacked the recipient
Natural killer cells reacted to excess MHC class I
quiz.explain: Minutes is far too fast for lymphocytes to be primed and expanded, so the effector must have been circulating before the operation. Preformed antibody binds the graft endothelium, fixes complement and clots the vessels at once.

lesson_media.alt: An adaptive-immunity network runs from antigen presentation to selection and expansion of a matching clone, then branches into immediate effector cells and persistent memory cells.
lesson_media.caption: Specificity exists before exposure; antigen expands a matching clone, whose descendants take parallel effector and memory fates under help, tolerance, and regulation.

nodes.title: Computational Biology
nodes.goal: Algorithms for sequence, structure and evolution.

quiz.prompt: A human gene and a mouse gene are 85 percent identical across 1,500 bases of coding sequence. Which conclusion is best supported?
quiz.answer: They descend from a single ancestral gene
quiz.explain: Identity that high over that length is far beyond anything chance alignment produces, and shared ancestry is the ordinary explanation. Homology does not guarantee identical function, and direct transfer between mammals is not a live possibility.
choices: They descend from a single ancestral gene
One genome recently acquired the gene from the other
Similarity at that level arises easily by chance
They must carry out exactly the same function

quiz.prompt: A bacterial genome containing many near-identical repeated regions assembles from short reads into far more, and far shorter, contigs than a repeat-free genome of the same size. Why?
quiz.answer: Reads from different copies look identical
quiz.explain: A read shorter than the repeat could have come from any copy, so the assembler cannot tell which flanking sequence belongs with which and breaks the contig there. This is exactly the problem long reads were developed to solve.
choices: Repeated regions are harder for the sequencer to read accurately
Reads from different copies look identical
Repeats mutate faster, so their reads disagree
Repeated DNA is present at lower coverage

quiz.prompt: A phylogenetic tree built from sequence data places two species in distant clades, yet the two share an unusual anatomical trait. Which reading does the tree favour?
quiz.answer: The trait arose twice over, independently
quiz.explain: Given the tree, either the trait evolved twice or it evolved once in a distant ancestor and was then lost along every intervening lineage. Both are possible, and the account needing fewer changes wins; across distant clades that is normally the double origin.
choices: The trait was inherited from their common ancestor and lost elsewhere
The trait arose twice over, independently
The two species must belong in one clade after all
The sequence data must have been misaligned

quiz.prompt: A BLAST search reports a hit with an E-value of 0.001. Across 1000 equivalent searches, how many hits this strong would you expect to arise by chance alone?
quiz.explain: The E-value is the number of chance hits expected per search, so 1000 x 0.001 = 1 expected chance hit.

quiz.prompt: Overfitting is a model capturing noise peculiar to its training set, so that it generalises poorly. A protein-function classifier scores 99 percent on its training proteins and 55 percent on a held-out set. Which change is most likely to help?
quiz.answer: Simplify the model or add more training data
choices: Add more parameters so it can fit the held-out set too
Report the training score, which is the honest one
Simplify the model or add more training data
Train for many more rounds on the same data
quiz.explain: The cure for fitting noise is less freedom or more signal: fewer parameters, regularisation, or more independent examples. More parameters and more rounds on the same data deepen the memorisation, and the training score is the one number that cannot detect it.

quiz.prompt: An RNA-seq study tests 20,000 genes at p < 0.05 and reports 800 significant hits. What should the analyst point out first?
quiz.answer: About 1000 hits are expected by chance alone at that threshold
choices: Simply ranking the hits and reporting the top ones is enough
About 1000 hits are expected by chance alone at that threshold
Testing more genes lowers the risk of false positives
A p-value under 0.05 shows that the genes are causal
quiz.explain: At alpha 0.05 across 20,000 tests you expect roughly 1,000 false positives, so 800 hits is fewer than chance alone would deliver. Nothing follows until the threshold is corrected for the number of tests.

quiz.prompt: A study tests 10,000 hypotheses and wants a family-wise error rate of 0.05 using a Bonferroni correction. Give the per-test significance threshold.
quiz.explain: Bonferroni divides the target rate by the number of tests: 0.05 / 10,000 = 5 x 10 to the power -6.

quiz.prompt: Two protein sequences of length 500 are aligned with no gaps and 60 mismatched positions. Give the percentage identity.
quiz.explain: Matching positions are 500 - 60 = 440, and 440/500 = 88 percent.

quiz.prompt: An aligner is run with an enormous gap-opening penalty on two homologous proteins that genuinely differ by a 20-residue insertion. What will the alignment most likely look like?
quiz.answer: The insertion appears as scattered mismatches
choices: The insertion is reported as a single longer gap
The insertion appears as scattered mismatches
The alignment score is unaffected by the penalty
The two sequences fail to align anywhere
quiz.explain: Scoring parameters shape the answer. Make a gap prohibitively expensive and the algorithm buys mismatches instead, sliding the sequences past each other and hiding the real insertion.

quiz.prompt: A structure predictor scores excellently on targets with close homologues in its training data but poorly on a protein with no known relatives. Which claim does this best support?
quiz.answer: Its accuracy leans on templates it has already seen
choices: Prediction is impossible without a template of some kind
Its accuracy leans on templates it has already seen
The orphan protein's experimental structure is in error
Its underlying physical energy function must be wrong
quiz.explain: A gap between homologue-rich and orphan targets is the standard diagnostic for how far a method is interpolating from known examples rather than reasoning from physics. It shows where the accuracy comes from, not that prediction without templates is impossible.

lesson_media.alt: A three-row computational biology pipeline maps sequences, structures, and evolutionary data to algorithms and explicitly limited biological hypotheses.
lesson_media.caption: Bioinformatics converts representations into ranked explanations; validation and uncertainty are part of the inference, not optional afterthoughts.

nodes.title: Frontiers of Biology
nodes.goal: Aging, the origin of life, and unsolved questions.

quiz.prompt: In the Miller-Urey experiment, sparks passed through a mixture of simple gases and water yielded several amino acids within a week. Which claim does this result most directly support?
quiz.answer: Life's building blocks can form without any life
quiz.explain: The flask produced monomers, not cells and not self-replication. What that supports is abiogenic chemistry: the units life is made of arise spontaneously under plausible prebiotic conditions, which is a long way short of an origin.
choices: Living cells were assembled in the flask from raw gases
Life's building blocks can form without any life
Amino acids are produced only by living organisms
The experiment settles how life on Earth began

quiz.prompt: Senescent cells stop dividing but secrete inflammatory signals. Clearing them from ageing mice improves several tissue measures. Which further result would most strengthen the claim that the secretions, rather than the loss of division, do the damage?
quiz.answer: Blocking the secretions alone helps as much
quiz.explain: Removing the cells takes away the secretions at the same time, so that experiment cannot separate the two. Leaving the cells in place while silencing what they secrete isolates the secretions as the agent.
choices: Clearing the cells also improves lifespan slightly
Blocking the secretions alone helps as much
Young mice have very few senescent cells at all
Senescent cells become more common with age

quiz.prompt: A mission budget allows one target. One team proposes a moon with a subsurface liquid ocean, another a hotter moon carrying only ice and vapour. Why do most astrobiologists back the first?
quiz.answer: All known life depends on liquid water
quiz.explain: Liquid water is the solvent every known biochemistry runs in: it dissolves and moves the molecules and lets them meet. Frozen water does none of that, and the case rests on what life is known to require, not on what is easy to detect.
choices: Any liquid would do; water is merely easiest to spot
All known life depends on liquid water
Water is needed as a source of oxygen to breathe
Ice supports the same chemistry as liquid water

quiz.prompt: A gene drive spreads to every individual in a caged mosquito population within 8 generations, each generation lasting 3 weeks. How many weeks did that take?
quiz.explain: 8 generations at 3 weeks each is 8 x 3 = 24 weeks.

quiz.prompt: A team edits a set of mammoth-like variants into an Asian elephant genome and produces a cold-tolerant calf. Why do most biologists resist calling it a mammoth?
quiz.answer: It is an edited elephant, not a recovered mammoth
choices: The calf was carried and born by an elephant mother
It is an edited elephant, not a recovered mammoth
The calf could not breed with a true mammoth
Mammoth DNA is too degraded ever to be read
quiz.explain: Editing a set of variants leaves the overwhelming majority of the genome, and all of the developmental and social context, elephant. Ancient mammoth genomes have in fact been sequenced, and the surrogate mother is beside the point either way.

quiz.prompt: Gene drives push an engineered allele through a wild population far faster than ordinary Mendelian inheritance. Give one benefit and one serious risk of releasing one.
quiz.answer: A drive could suppress the mosquitoes that spread malaria and save many lives, but once released it is very hard to control, can spread beyond the target population, and may disturb the wider ecosystem.
quiz.explain: The same property that makes a drive powerful, its ability to sweep through a population, is what makes release hard to reverse and ecologically risky.

quiz.prompt: A telomere loses about 50 base pairs each time a cell divides. Starting at 10,000 base pairs, how many divisions until it is down to 4,000?
quiz.explain: The loss needed is 10,000 - 4,000 = 6,000 base pairs, and 6,000 / 50 = 120 divisions.

quiz.prompt: A compound raises median lifespan in mice by 15 percent but leaves maximum lifespan unchanged. Which reading is best supported?
quiz.answer: It removes early deaths rather than slowing ageing
choices: It slows the ageing process across the whole population
It removes early deaths rather than slowing ageing
It shows that ageing has a single molecular cause
Its effect will be even larger in humans
quiz.explain: Squaring the survival curve while leaving its far end where it was is the signature of removing early causes of death. Genuinely slowing ageing would push the maximum out as well as the median.

quiz.prompt: A ribozyme is found that both stores sequence information and catalyses copying of itself. Why does that matter for origin-of-life research?
quiz.answer: One molecule could do both jobs at once
choices: It removes the need for natural selection early on
One molecule could do both jobs at once
It proves RNA was the first molecule to appear
It shows that membranes came later than RNA did
quiz.explain: The chicken-and-egg problem is that DNA needs proteins to be copied and proteins need DNA to be specified. A molecule that both carries the information and catalyses its own copying breaks that circle; it does not date RNA against membranes.

quiz.prompt: A returned Martian rock contains tiny rod-shaped structures and organic molecules. Why do most scientists hold back from calling it past life?
quiz.answer: Ordinary non-living chemistry can make both features
choices: Rod-shaped structures are always mineral, never fossil
Ordinary non-living chemistry can make both features
Organic molecules are found only inside living things
Only a living sample could ever count as evidence
quiz.explain: A biosignature has to be something non-living processes cannot readily produce. Both organic molecules and small rod-shaped mineral forms have well-documented abiotic routes, so neither settles anything on its own.

lesson_media.alt: A frontier-evidence matrix separates established observations, open mechanisms, and discriminating tests for origins of life, ageing, and extraterrestrial life.
lesson_media.caption: Unsolved biology advances when broad questions become competing, risky predictions that new data can distinguish.
